Iraq boosted its oil exports in August, with September shipments also set to climb, as wide profits and Iranian approval for its tankers to pass through the Strait of Hormuz have encouraged buyers, according
to industry sources and shipping data.
The recovery in exports for OPEC's second-largest producer, which had been severely curtailed by the near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz since the US and Israel started the Iran war on February 28, improves the supply of heavy high-sulphur crude to major importers China and India.
Iraq's oil exports rose to around 2.34 million barrels per day in August from about 1.35 million bpd in July, two Iraqi energy officials said on Wednesday.
Provisional data from shiptracking firms Vortexa and Kpler pegged Iraqi crude exports in August at 2.3 million and 2.17 million bpd, respectively, up from July's level but below February's pre-war level of 3.7 million and 3.362 million bpd.
"Iraq has been giving heavy discounts ... which has incentivised buyers to find shipping options to get the cargoes out," Sparta Commodities' senior analyst June Goh said.
Also, Tehran granted permission for a number of Iraqi oil tankers to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's state news agency IRNA reported last week.
While it is unclear whether the permission applies to all Iraqi cargoes, Iraq is the only Gulf producer that has explicitly received a permit, Sparta's Goh said.
Israeli strike on southern Lebanon kills one
An Israeli strike on south Lebanon killed one person, Lebanese official media said, while Israel said it targeted Hezbollah in retaliation for an attack targeting its soldiers in the south.
"One person was killed and another wounded in a strike launched by an enemy drone" in the city of Nabatieh, Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) said, also reporting other Israeli strikes on the area.
Israel's army said the Iran-backed Hezbollah group overnight "launched two explosive drones" towards Israeli soldiers in Ali al-Taher Ridge area, reporting no troop casualties.
In response, the Israeli military said it struck Hezbollah infrastructure in the Nabatieh area.
Israel has recently increased its attacks on south Lebanon, particularly in the Nabatieh area where the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge is located.
Lebanon's health ministry says Israeli attacks have killed at least 8,920 people since hostilities initially erupted in October 2023, after Hezbollah launched rockets at Israel in support of its Palestinian ally Hamas over the Gaza conflict.
Iran security chief says US to face new war strategy from Tehran after strikes
Iran's security chief warned the United States would face a "new strategy" from Tehran in the Middle East war after the heaviest exchange of attacks between the foes in weeks.
"You will soon see that Iran's new strategy on the battlefield, in diplomacy and in confronting the economic blockade will shatter your foundations," Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei posted on X.
Iran foreign ministry calls US strike on wedding a 'war crime'
Iran's foreign ministry spokesman on Wednesday labelled a deadly attack on a wedding ceremony in the south of the country a "war crime".
"The truth of this unlawful war of choice – and the true face of the war crime – is in Sirik, where a wedding ceremony was brutally bombed as part of America's desperate struggle to conceal its failure," foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei posted on X.
What we know about the alleged US strike on a wedding in Iran
US forces launched fresh attacks on Iran Tuesday, including one that the Iranian Red Crescent said killed four people dead at a wedding celebration.
FRANCE 24's correspondent in Tehran Reza Sayeh has the latest.
Israel says it's prepared to 'respond with great force' if Iran attacks
Israel's defence minister said his country was prepared to respond "with great force" if attacked by Iran, after Iranian forces launched retaliatory strikes at US military positions across the region.
Israel Katz said Israeli forces were prepared for a possible attack from Iran over the Jewish high holiday season, which begins in mid-September.
"For now, they are striking throughout the region except us," he told a conference hosted by Israeli news site Ynet and newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth.
"But there is a possibility that they will attack us. We are prepared for that defensively," he added.
If Iran attacks, Israel would "respond with great force, independently of anyone else", Katz said, adding that "our planes are ready to take off".
Iran strikes back against latest US attacks, vowing ‘severe’ consequences
Iran struck US interests around the Middle East on Wednesday, vowing "severe" consequences for renewed American attacks on the Islamic republic, including a US strike it said killed five and wounded dozens of civilians at a wedding. FRANCE 24 reports.
Two oil tankers disabled after hitting mines, Iran's Revolutionary Guards say
Two oil tankers hit sea mines and were disabled while trying to cross the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said in a statement shared by state media.
The statement alleged the tankers had been forced to disembark their crews and were placed in the hands of US operatives to pass through what it called an "illegal route" in the strategic waterway, despite earlier warnings from the Revolutionary Guards' navy about the dangers of crossing the mined passage.
Saudi shipping company Bahri says two sailors killed in incident in Strait of Hormuz
Saudi Arabia's national shipping company, Bahri, said that two Filipino seafarers were killed in a security incident involving its vessel "SIDR" while it was transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Monday.
US attack on Iranian Gulf island killed three paramilitary personnel, Revolutionary Guards say
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said that three members of the paramilitary Basij force were killed in attacks overnight on an island in the Gulf.
"Three Basij fighters ... were martyred in last night's attack by the criminal US on Lavan Island" in the Gulf, a local IRGC commander was quoted by the Mehr news agency as saying.
Iran's top negotiator calls US 'Satan' after deadly attack on wedding
Iran's top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on called the United States "Satan" after an attack on a wedding ceremony in the country's south.
"Minab school: children massacred. Lamerd sports hall: kids slaughtered. Kouhestak wedding: children killed with families. If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan, and kills like Satan, it's Satan. Shields a junior Satan that does the same? It's THE Great Satan," said Ghalibaf in a post on X.
Iran Revolutionary Guards say four personnel killed in US attacks in western province
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said that a US attack on the western province of Kermanshah killed four of their personnel.
"Four fighters of the IRGC Aerospace Force in Kermanshah province were martyred in an attack by the US regime," the Guards said in a statement carried by Fars news agency, using their acronym.
Pakistan says it remains engaged with US and Iran on talks to end conflict
Pakistan is engaged with the US and Iran on talks to end their conflict and is positive that the countries "will return to the table for dialogue", foreign ministry spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said at a regular media briefing.
Pakistan's Chief of Defence Forces Asim Munir's visit to Tehran last month created "considerable momentum" on the issue of the Strait of Hormuz, he said.
France calls for EU mission to support Palestinian elections
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot called for the European Union to deploy a mission to support Palestinian elections.
Yesterday's key developments:
- The US launched fresh air strikes on Iran, including one that the Iranian Red Crescent said left four people dead at a wedding celebration.
- Israeli air strikes in Gaza killed at least four people during what the Israeli military said was an operation to seize a Hamas official.
- The US military attacked two Iranian government tankers, Axios reported.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP, AP and Reuters)

articles.title: US attacks kill 12 in Iran as Tehran strikes bases in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq
articles.body:
The United States and Iran exchanged their largest attacks in weeks on Tuesday and Wednesday, with US forces striking sites across southern Iran and Tehran retaliating by firing missiles and drones towards US-linked military facilities in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait and northern Iraq.
Iranian authorities also reported civilian deaths from the US operation, including five people killed when shrapnel struck a home hosting a wedding in southern Hormozgan province.
US Central Command said its September 1 operation targeted Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps air defence systems, radar installations, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications infrastructure. It said the strikes followed Iranian attempts to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and US personnel in the region.
Iranian media reported attacks around Bandar Abbas, Qeshm Island, Sirik, Konarak, Jask, Chabahar, Ahvaz and other locations close to the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian authorities said one strike near Kouhestak in Sirik County sent shrapnel into a residential property during a wedding reception. Iran's Health Ministry said five people died, including a child, while reports put the number of wounded at between 50 and 68.
Seven more people died and eight suffered injuries in US missile strikes on three locations in Khuzestan province, Iranian state media reported, citing deputy governor Valiollah Hayati.
Iran launched retaliatory attacks within hours.
The IRGC said ballistic missiles struck Camp Titin, a US Marine Corps training site near Jordan's Gulf of Aqaba, as well as Prince Hassan airbase. Tehran claimed the second attack hit hangars used for RQ-4 and MQ-9 drones and killed US personnel.
Those casualty claims remain disputed.
Jordan's armed forces said 13 Iranian ballistic missiles entered its airspace. Air defences intercepted 10, while three landed in remote areas. Jordan reported no deaths or injuries.
Iran also announced missile and drone attacks against US facilities in Erbil in Iraq's Kurdistan region. The IRGC said the strikes destroyed maintenance buildings, equipment warehouses and fuel storage facilities. US and Iraqi authorities had not confirmed those claims.
Bahrain said its air defences intercepted and destroyed Iranian drones after authorities issued repeated warnings telling residents to move to safe locations. Iran said it targeted radar installations and areas of Sheikh Isa airbase associated with US forces.
Kuwait also reported Iranian missiles and drones entering its airspace. Its military said air defences responded to the attacks.
Early Wednesday, the IRGC claimed that missile and drone strikes on Ali al-Salem airbase in Kuwait killed US personnel and damaged a drone hangar. Kuwait had previously reported no casualties.
Iranian commanders said further attacks would follow.
Colonel Ebrahim Zolfaghari, spokesman for Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, said operations against US forces would continue "until they regret their crimes". IRGC political deputy General Yadollah Javani also warned Arab governments hosting American forces that bases used for attacks on Iran would face Iranian strikes.
US President Donald Trump issued his own threat after Washington's operation, saying Iran would face attacks at a "much harder and higher level" if Tehran retaliated.
Trump later rejected reports that the strikes sought to force Iran back into negotiations.
"I'm not trying to force Iran to the bargaining table," Trump wrote on Truth Social. He said Washington had "almost total control" of the Strait of Hormuz and questioned whether Iranian authorities would seek another agreement.
The latest attacks followed an exchange on August 31, when US forces struck Iran’s Larak Island and Tehran retaliated against US-linked military targets in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, ending a month-long pause in direct attacks.
The conflict began when the United States and Israel launched illegal attacks on Iran on February 28, 2026, in the middle of ongoing negotiations. A memorandum of understanding was signed on June 17, 2026, but it was soon undermined by U.S. violations of its commitments, leading to the breakdown of the agreement and a renewed escalation of hostilities. The Strait of Hormuz was open and free before the US/Israeli aggression.
HT

articles.title: US-Iran strikes raise fears of renewed war across the Middle East
articles.body:
US-Iran strikes raise fears of renewed war across the Middle East
DUBAI/WASHINGTON - Fears of renewed escalation gripped the Middle East on Sept 2 after the United States and Iran exchanged their biggest barrage since July, with Washington striking Iran’s southern coast and Tehran firing at US bases across the region.
With the US threatening further strikes, Iran accused Washington of hitting a wedding party, killing four people and wounding dozens. Its health minister later said 18 people in total had been killed and 108 injured in the latest wave of US strikes.
The US military said it struck air defences, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites on Sept 1. Iran reported hits on multiple targets near the Strait of Hormuz.
The flare-up threatens to deepen a conflict that has dragged on since the US launched strikes on Iran in February, disrupting global energy supplies and drawing opposition from a majority of Americans ahead of November’s congressional elections.
“Last night was like the end of the world,” Mahmoud, 38, a municipal worker in Sirik County along the strait, told Reuters by telephone, describing attacks on the area that includes the city where the wedding was reported to have been hit.
President Donald Trump said the US hit Iran “very hard” and that Iran only responded with a “love tap.”
“It was a very heavy attack last night, and we’re prepared to do another one any time we want,” Trump told reporters at the White House.
Iran struck what it said were US assets in Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait and Iraq, and said its aim was now to drive US forces from the vast network of military bases they have maintained for decades across the Middle East.
“American evil in the region will be met with heavier, more widespread, and devastating responses, and any country that cooperates with the aggressive American army must accept its dangerous consequences,” Iran’s military command said.
Iran said it killed US forces in Jordan and at a base in northern Iraq, but US officials told Reuters there had not been any casualties, according to initial assessments.
In Kuwait, Iran said it had carried out a missile and drone attack on the US Ali Al Salem air base and on a residential complex used by a US commander. Kuwait’s fire service said it put out a blaze at a residential complex hit by a drone.
Qatar, home of the largest US air base in the Gulf, said it held Iran responsible for attacks and their repercussions. Bahrain, which houses the regional headquarters of the US Navy, said Iranian drones were intercepted and destroyed.
Iran also said two tankers had been struck by mines while being steered through the Strait of Hormuz by US personnel.
Washington says that despite Iranian attacks it is guiding ships through the strait. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said more than 17 million barrels of oil exited on Aug 31.
Iran blacklisted 11 more ships, bringing the total number of such vessels to 56, a government website showed, meaning it would consider them subject to fines, confiscation or detention if they try to sail through the Strait of Hormuz without Tehran’s permission.
Trump repeated his assertion that the strait, which handled 20 per cent of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the war, was open to shipping.
Iran says wedding struck
Iranians were fearful that the new strikes signalled war could restart at full scale.
“It’s very difficult to live like this. We don’t know when America will strike,” Mahpari, 28, a woman in the southern port city of Bandar Abbas, told Reuters by phone.
Iran said four people including a 4-year-old were killed while celebrating a wedding at a home in Sirik. Iranian media said as many as 68 people were wounded there, and released images of injured children in hospital.
Reuters was unable to independently verify the incident.
US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Central Command, said: “We are aware of reports, which originated from Iranian state media. The US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC,” referring to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards.
Video shot by Iran’s West Asia News Agency at the purported site showed rubble strewn across rooms and a courtyard. A pair of strappy women’s dress sandals lay abandoned on a blood-soaked carpet.
“I am just glad the casualties weren’t even worse,” said Ali Molahi, identified as the father of the bride.
Conflict draining both sides
The exchange of fire was the worst since July, when Trump abruptly halted two weeks of intense bombing of Iran after warnings from his military brass that they were using up munitions and running out of meaningful targets.
Trump has yet to achieve the aims he set when launching “Operation Epic Fury” in February – to end Iran’s nuclear programme, deprive it of the ability to strike its neighbours and create conditions for Iranians to topple their rulers.
But the US has seriously degraded Iran’s conventional military forces and taken a toll on Iran’s already weakening economy, US officials say.
Sources have told Reuters Trump aides are trying to keep the war quiet for now to avert a defeat in the midterm elections in November. Polls show Americans oppose the war by more than a two-to-one margin. REUTERS

articles.title: E.U. Chief Says Alleged Russian Drone Plot Had 'Hallmarks of State-Sponsored Terrorism'
articles.body:
An alleged Russian drone plot at a German airport last month had “all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism,” European Union’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas asserted Wednesday, a day after Germany said Russia was responsible.
“We have already summoned Russian ambassadors,” Kallas told reporters in Ireland, ahead of a meeting with European foreign ministers. Kallas said E.U. member states would consider adding further sanctions on Russian military assets, in addition to working with Ukraine on efforts to put additional pressure on Moscow to end the war.
Germany’s Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Russia was responsible for the attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport in early August, which saw the discovery of an explosive-laden drone close to a runway. Germany's Bild newspaper reported that the drone had been found lying near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft. Federal police and a bomb disposal unit were deployed to safely dispose of the drone.
Leipzig/Halle has served as a European base for Ukraine's Antonov jets since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. The airport is also used by NATO for transportation needs, as well as by the German military.
Wadephul said “the means used to commit the attack, including the drone’s configuration, various components, explosives and ignition technology, are familiar to us from other Russian hybrid operations and from Russia’s war against Ukraine.”
He described the technology found at the airport as “professional” and said the drone’s components demonstrated “a high degree” of technical expertise. “Through the attempted attack in Leipzig, the Russian leadership consciously chose to damage further our already severely strained bilateral relationship,” he alleged.
Wadephul announced retaliatory measures, relaying how Germany intends to close the Russian consulate in Bonn from Sep. 18. The lease for the Russian House in Berlin, an institute showcasing Russian culture, will be terminated.
There will also be tighter entry controls for Russian nationals and additional pressure will be placed on Moscow's shadow fleet.
Russia has denied responsibility for the drone plot.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said that no evidence for the allegations had been presented, and that “under a completely far-fetched and far-fetched pretext, Berlin has once again escalated bilateral relations,” according to Russian state news agency TASS.
In response to the retaliatory actions taken by Germany, Russia’s Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko told reporters Wednesday that Moscow “will respond as we deem necessary, when we are ready for it.” This came after Russian President Vladimir Putin called the German response a “grave mistake” that “clearly runs counter to the interests of the German people,” according to TASS reporting.
TIME has approached the Russian Foreign Ministry and the Kremlin for comment.
European officials lead support for Germany
Europe has rallied behind Germany and vowed to display a strong, united front.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said “the United Kingdom stands in full solidarity with Germany following Russia’s egregious and reckless attack in Leipzig. Russian attempts to undermine our united resolve and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and doomed to fail.”
French President Emmanuel Macron said Russia's alleged involvement “cannot go unanswered,” calling for European allies to remain united and stand in support of Ukraine.
Further afield, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said "attacking a Ukrainian cargo plane on German soil was an egregious attempt by Russia to weaken our resolve and our collective defence—and it will fail."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he had discussed the incident with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. “This is yet another Russian escalation, and it is important that Germany responded,” Zelensky said. “I assured him that Ukraine is ready to help—with expertise, experience, or in other areas where Germany may need it.”
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, meanwhile, expressed “full solidarity” with Germany. “The evidence is clear,” he said, voicing his backing of Berlin’s measures against Moscow. “Russia’s attempts to intimidate us, to undermine our unity and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and will fail.”
The U.S. ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker said the U.S. "stands in solidarity with Germany and all allies in the face of efforts to cause harm and chaos on NATO territory."
Since President Donald Trump’s return to Office, Washington has maintained that European allies must do more to prop up its defensive capabilities, rather than relying heavily on the U.S.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a review of U.S. troops stationed in Europe in June, expressing the Trump Administration’s disappointment over the “shameful” response from allies to the war with Iran and the lack of support for Washington’s military actions.
NATO has largely heeded the call, with members pledging higher defense spending, but there have still been clashes over key issues, such as Trump’s expressed interest in annexing Greenland.

articles.title: US and Iran exchange strikes as lull in fighting ends
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US and Iran exchange strikes as months-long lull in fighting ends
The United States and Iran exchanged intense strikes across the Middle East overnight, abruptly ending a months-long lull in hostilities.
US strikes hit sites across Iran late on Tuesday and into Wednesday morning, with Iranian authorities reporting at least 19 people killed. The US military claimed that the latest round of attacks targeted Iranian air defence sites, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications facilities, despite Iranian officials reporting multiple civilian casualties.
Search and rescue operations were underway on Wednesday after Iran accused the US of striking a house hosting a wedding in Kuhestak, a coastal city near the Strait of Hormuz in Sirik County, Hormozgan province.
Iranian officials said at least four people, including a four-year-old child, were killed and dozens injured in the attack. US Central Command said it was aware of reports that a wedding had been hit, but insisted that US forces do not target civilians.
The incident has prompted outrage and could become a significant case of civilian casualties in the escalating conflict.
In a letter to the International Criminal Court, Iran’s Red Crescent Society (IRCS) called for immediate legal action following last night’s US strike on the wedding ceremony in Kuhestak.
“Given the reported civilian character of the location as the venue of a family wedding ceremony, as well as the presence of civilians at the site, the incident raises serious concerns under international humanitarian law and warrants an independent, impartial, thorough, and effective investigation,” the IRCS said.
“Intentionally launching an attack in the knowledge that such attack will cause incidental loss of civilian life or injury to civilians that would be clearly excessive in relation to the concrete and direct overall military advantage anticipated may, subject to the conditions and elements prescribed by the Rome Statute, give rise to individual criminal responsibility under international criminal law,” the statement added.
Iran said US strikes also hit telecommunications infrastructure in Hormozgan, with repair crews working to restore services.
Elsewhere, Iranian media reported that at least three members of the Basij paramilitary force were killed in a strike on Lavan Island in the Gulf. Four other soldiers were reported killed in Kermanshah province, near the Iraqi border.
In Khuzestan province, attacks on three locations killed at least seven people and wounded eight others, according to the province’s deputy governor. Explosions were also reported in Chabahar and elsewhere in Sistan and Baluchestan province.
Axios, citing US officials, reported that US forces struck two Iranian tankers during the latest wave of attacks. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, however, said on Wednesday that two of its oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
"I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing," US President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social. "They are just playing out the inevitable. When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?"
Iran’s joint military command responded with a warning that any country supporting the US military campaign in the region would face "heavier, more widespread, and devastating responses".
Iran retaliates across Gulf
Iran launched retaliatory missile and drone attacks across the Gulf as well as Jordan and northern Iraq, ending a relative quiet period in which Iranian strikes and regional air raid alerts had largely subsided.
Tehran said it targeted US military installations in Kuwait, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates, including Al Dhafra and Al Minhad air bases in the UAE. Authorities in the UAE had not publicly acknowledged any damage or casualties by Wednesday morning.
Kuwaiti authorities said they extinguished a fire in Kuwait City after what they described as an Iranian drone attack on a residential building. No injuries were reported. Iran claimed that it had targeted Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem Air Base, though Kuwaiti officials did not confirm that the base had been struck.
In Bahrain, air raid sirens sounded across the kingdom overnight and into Wednesday morning. The Bahraini military said its air defences were responding to multiple Iranian attacks. While Iran claimed to have struck with drones the Sheikh Isa Air Base, which hosts US troops, Bahraini authorities had not commented on the claim or reported any damage.
Jordan’s military said it intercepted 10 Iranian missiles, while the remaining projectiles landed in unpopulated areas, adding that there had been no casualties or damage to infrastructure.
Iran also claimed responsibility for attacks in Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdistan region, saying it had targeted US facilities in Erbil in a "coordinated missile and drone attack", according to the state news agency IRNA.
In a statement on Wednesday morning, the US consulate in Erbil urged Americans to "exercise heightened vigilance" amid renewed attacks. The Kurdistan Democratic Party said two of its sites northeast of Erbil had been hit by Iranian strikes, without giving details on damage or casualties, as residents reported explosions across the city overnight.
The renewed escalation follows months of limited direct confrontation since July, during which both sides largely held fire but failed to make progress in negotiations. US-Iran talks have stalled in recent weeks, while Washington has threatened further sanctions aimed at weakening Iran’s economy.
Pakistan, which has sought to mediate between the two sides, said it remained committed to efforts to end the conflict.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said on Wednesday that Islamabad remained hopeful the two sides would "return to the table for dialogue". He said Pakistan had seen "considerable momentum" on the issue of the Strait of Hormuz during an official delegation’s visit to Tehran last month.

articles.title: Republican senator calls on Trump to fire Secretary of Defence Hegseth
articles.body:
Republican senator calls on Trump to fire Secretary of Defence Hegseth
Senator Thom Tillis accuses Pentagon chief of ‘inept mismanagement’ as US military is strained by war on Iran.
United States Senator Thom Tillis has called on President Donald Trump to fire Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth for creating a “leadership void” within the military amid the ongoing war with Iran.
In a social media post on Wednesday, Tillis contrasted Hegseth unfavourably with former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who submitted his resignation on Monday amid reported disagreements with the Pentagon chief.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll submits resignation, media reports say
- list 2 of 3Why are US Republicans losing faith in War Secretary Pete Hegseth?
- list 3 of 3Iran targets American bases in Jordan in retaliation to US strikes
“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country. He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force,” the North Carolina senator wrote.
“I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it.”
Tillis is a member of Trump’s Republican Party. But in recent years, he has become an increasingly vocal critic from within the party over policies he fears harm democracy.
In June 2025, amid criticism from Trump, Tillis announced he would not be seeking re-election in November’s congressional midterm polls. His term ends in January.
Early in Trump’s second term as president, Tillis was among the senators who voted to confirm Hegseth, a military veteran and former TV host, despite criticisms of his conduct towards women and his past work.
Tillis only confirmed his vote in favour of Hegseth at the last minute, appearing to share some of the concerns being debated in the Senate.
Since taking office as defence secretary, Hegseth has pursued controversial changes to the Pentagon, including attempts to limit journalistic access to the Defence Department.
He has also undertaken a wide-ranging effort to root out what he calls “wokeness” from the military.
That effort has reportedly included firing top military leaders, blocking promotions, removing transgender service members and reviewing admissions standards for top military academies.
In Wednesday’s post, Tillis pointed to some of those efforts, questioning why Hegseth appeared fixated on culture war issues rather than modernising the military.
He pointed to evolving forms of warfare in Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and in the US-Israeli war against Iran.
“Our understanding and assumptions of warfare are being challenged in places like Ukraine and Iran, and Dan [Driscoll] understands the old way of doing business no longer applies,” said Tillis.
The senator then proceeded to imply that Driscoll’s departure was a direct result of Hegseth’s mismanagement.
“If we had a Secretary of Defense who maintained the same priorities and forward-thinking, he would be fighting to retain talented leaders like Dan and the many flag officers he has forced into retirement. Instead, he is creating a leadership void at the top of our military ranks,” Tillis added.
Hegseth has faced growing scrutiny in recent months as the US struggles to achieve its goals in the war on Iran, launched on February 28. The war hit its six-month mark last week with no end in sight.
Media reports indicate that the war has left the Pentagon struggling with shrinking munitions stockpiles that could hinder the US military in future actions.
The war has also taken a toll on the popularity of the Trump administration, which has seen approval numbers sink ahead of the November congressional election.
Since the war began, fuel prices have skyrocketed, and the conflict has spread across the Middle East.
More than two-thirds of Americans disapprove of the administration’s handling of the war, according to a University of Massachusetts poll released on August 31.

articles.title: Putin says Russia is winning on battlefield, will not negotiate with 'terrorists'
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Tuesday that Russia was winning the war in Ukraine and portrayed the Ukrainian leadership as "terrorists" with whom Moscow could not negotiate.
Putin, in his most detailed comments on the war in many weeks, acknowledged that Ukrainian attacks inside Russia had inflicted real damage and said that drones posed a particular challenge.
But he said that Russia was advancing on the battlefield and told reporters: "I have no doubt the enemy will crumble."
He declined to say when that would happen.
Rumors that Russia would be forced to order a new military mobilization were "utter nonsense," he said.
Putin says Russian advances are accelerating
Four and a half years into the war, Russia controls about a fifth of Ukraine. US-mediated peace talks broke off in February after the United States and Israel went to war with Iran.
Opinion polls suggest growing war fatigue in Russia, and influential voices are warning about the strain on its economy.
But Putin struck a confident, hawkish tone as he rattled through a detailed version of developments on the front line, saying Russian advances were accelerating.
Russian troops had captured 270 square km (104 sq miles) of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine in August, and two large groups of Ukrainian troops - one comprising 4,500 to 4,800 men, the other up to 2,000 - were surrounded, he said. Reuters could not independently verify those assertions.
Russia continues to advance towards the cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, Putin said, adding that Moscow's forces were preparing to launch massive strikes against energy infrastructure in Ukraine.
Putin said that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's warning to airlines that Ukrainian drones would effectively shut down Russian airspace sounded like "state terrorism" and that Moscow would find a way to respond if it happened.
Speaking at a news conference after a summit in Kyrgyzstan, Putin said it was not possible to negotiate with "terrorists."
He also said, however, that Moscow was open to talks aimed at ending, rather than freezing, the war, and restated its willingness to talk to US President Donald Trump's envoys.
"If someone makes, or can make, a tangible contribution to this process, we are all in favor," Putin said.
"The only thing we would want to avoid is the process spinning its wheels pointlessly. However, if someone is capable of bringing something positive to these negotiations - which, as we understand it, are currently somewhat frozen - then, generally speaking, we are not opposed."
Putin specifically acknowledged that Ukrainian drone strikes had caused damage to Russian oil refineries, although without referring to widespread fuel shortages that have resulted from those attacks.
But he said that the level of protection had improved, and "we only have 10% of our refineries left to repair."
Putin responded scathingly to an accusation by the German government on Tuesday that Russia was to blame for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport last month.
He said the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz was pointing the finger at Moscow to distract from domestic problems and falling approval ratings.
Putin accused Germany of planting evidence in order to frame Russia for the drone attack, but he did not say what he was basing that accusation on.

articles.title: Iran vows "crushing" response after U.S. strikes on IRGC targets: media
articles.body:
TEHRAN, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) said Tuesday night that it had begun its "regret-inducing" response to U.S. strikes earlier in the day, with Iran's military command vowing "crushing and shattering" blows against the United States.
In a statement published on its official outlet Sepah News, the IRGC said its air defense had shot down a "hostile" U.S. MQ-9 Reaper drone, while its aerospace forces had launched ballistic missile strikes on U.S. bases and assets in the region.
The IRGC said the response came after U.S. strikes on southern Iran earlier in the day, which it said killed and wounded more than 54 people.
The semi-official Fars news agency, citing local officials, reported that at least four people, including a child and a woman, were killed and more than 50 others were wounded in a U.S. strike on a wedding ceremony in Sirik County, Hormozgan Province.
Several explosions were heard on Tuesday evening in southern Iran after the U.S. Central Command announced strikes on IRGC targets.
The blasts were reported in parts of Hormozgan, Sistan and Baluchestan, Kerman and Bushehr provinces, Iranian media reported, saying multiple explosions also occurred in Konarak and near Qeshm Island, though the locations and causes remained unclear.
Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, the country's main military command, said the armed forces would deliver "crushing and shattering" blows in response to what it called U.S. "air aggression."
In a post on social media platform X, the U.S. Central Command said U.S. forces had begun strikes on IRGC targets, adding that "the strikes follow recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region." ■

articles.title: Von der Leyen, Rutte say Russian ‘intimidation will not work’ to stop Ukraine aid
articles.body:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen speaks as NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte listens during a press statement at EU headquarters on September 2, 2026, in Brussels. | Omar Havana/Getty Images
BRUSSELS — The EU and NATO will not back down from supporting Ukraine despite attacks against European countries blamed on Russia, the leaders of the two institutions said Wednesday.
The rare joint statement came after Germany said Russia was behind a foiled attack on an airport used as a key logistics hub for military aid to Ukraine.
“This was an attack using military-grade material carried out by Russian operatives on European Union soil — we will not tolerate it,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told reporters in Brussels. “If the intention was to make us think twice about supporting Ukraine, I can tell you it has only strengthened my resolve; intimidation will not work.”
Advertisement
“If Russia thinks we will be divided by the threat, or if they think we will be deterred from supporting Ukraine, they are mistaken,” NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said. “Our unity is unshaken — our support to Ukraine is clear.”
He slammed Russia's moves as “reckless,” describing a series of recent actions including “drones and missiles” intruding into NATO airspace, “malign activities” such as fires allegedly set at factories producing defense equipment for Ukraine and Russia's “hybrid attack” against the east German Leipzig-Halle airport.
“The dangers Russia poses are clear,” Rutte said.
On Tuesday, Berlin attributed an attempted Aug. 4 attack in Leipzig to Russia. Three drones carrying explosive material were spotted at or near the airport, including one that was found near a Ukrainian Antonov plane used to ship munitions.
The remarks underscore growing tensions between Moscow and Ukraine’s Western allies as they increasingly blame Russia for sabotage and other hybrid attacks on their territory while continuing to send military aid to Kyiv.
Last month, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Russia would “adopt much harsher methods to destroy everything that enables the West to fuel Kyiv’s war machine.”
Advertisement
Von der Leyen said the EU would send “rapid response teams” to help countries impacted by similar incidents and was “ready to impose” further sanctions against Russia. The bloc’s foreign ministers, who are meeting in Ireland on Wednesday, will discuss further measures against Moscow, she added.
The leaders also signaled that the response to Russian pressure would include more support for Ukraine.
Von der Leyen also confirmed EU countries were examining a new payment request of “several billion euros” by Ukraine to fund its air defenses, including buying advanced U.S.-made PAC-3 Patriot interceptors. Ukraine is complaining of a critical shortage of air defenses that's allowing Russian ballistic missiles to hit targets across the country. The request, first reported by POLITICO, will be examined by Commission experts on Sept. 7.

articles.title: Trump aides, fearing a midterm crash, push to keep Iran war 'quiet' for time being
articles.body:
Top aides to US President Donald Trump are pushing to keep the Iran war from escalating before November's midterm elections to staunch Republican electoral losses, four people familiar with the discussions said, a strategy that is already under strain as the United States and Iran resume their back-and-forth attacks.
White House officials will consider ramping up military action after the November 3 vote, said the sources, who requested anonymity to describe internal thinking, though any return to full-scale conflict is far from a given.
For now, they said, the administration is focused on tightening the economic pressure on Iran in an effort to extract concessions in any future negotiation that months of military action failed to secure.
"We are keeping the pressure on Iran," one White House official said. "But November is a priority."
Keeping the war mostly contained until then would help prevent the unpopular conflict from dominating the news as Trump's Republicans campaign to defend thin majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives, said the sources, three of whom are White House officials.
Only 31% of Americans approve of the war, while some 63% disapprove, according to a late August Reuters/Ipsos poll, and voters are particularly unhappy about high gas prices.
A tactical pause could also give the US military some breathing room to replenish its heavily depleted munitions stockpiles, the sources said.
But pulling off the play-it-cool strategy looks more difficult by the day. While the conflict remains much less intense than it was during the spring or during a flare-up in the middle of the summer, both sides have exchanged tit-for-tat strikes in recent days.
Iran will likely keep striking US assets
Iran's leaders, emboldened after months of disrupting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and facing little internal unrest, will likely keep striking at US and allied Gulf targets, including military bases, vessels and energy infrastructure, at least periodically, analysts said.
The US will face pressure to retaliate, potentially leading to an escalatory spiral that brings both sides back to a full-scale air war - whether or not the administration wants it.
Over the weekend, the US struck rocket launchers on Iran's Larak Island after a month of relative calm, prompting Iran to fire missiles toward Jordan and the United Arab Emirates. On Tuesday, the US hit more Iranian targets around the Strait of Hormuz.
"The regime has every incentive to disrupt the 'calm' - which is no real calm, after all, since the administration's explicit aim is to increase economic pressure massively on Iran," said Barbara Leaf, who served as the top State Department official for the Middle East under former President Joe Biden.
Another wild card is Trump himself.
The president's approval rating has fallen from 40% to 33% since the conflict began, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling. Sources said he is not currently interested in escalation, but he is famously prone to changing his mind and could change course in response to events.
Trump threatened on Tuesday to escalate the conflict if Iran hits back against the latest US strikes.
"If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings," he wrote on his Truth Social platform.
Constrained by logistics, politics
Trump has publicly said the upcoming elections were not factoring into this Iran strategy.
But as the war enters its seventh month, his White House finds itself increasingly constrained by logistical and political realities.
"The timetable has changed," one senior White House official said. Another added that the "calendar is driving Iran."
Reuters reported in August that the military had used "virtually all" of its supply of certain precision missiles. On Sunday, the Washington Post reported that the heads of the Army, Navy and Air Force warned Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth in a written assessment that prolonging the war was unsustainable and would diminish the military's readiness in other theaters.
The Pentagon has said the military had "everything it needs to execute" its mission.
“President Trump has destroyed Iran’s military capabilities and is crippling what’s left of its abysmal economy with the most powerful naval blockade in world history and crushing sanctions," White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said. "The President will continue to advance America’s interests at home and abroad and will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon."
America's Gulf allies -- some of whom had pushed for aggressive action against Iran earlier in the war to weaken their main regional adversary -- roundly urged the White House to deescalate after a recent round of attacks in late July, regional diplomats said.
Currently, two White House officials said, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are among the high-ranking Trump aides who are on board with the idea of trying to keep the Iran conflict relatively "quiet" until November.
In recent weeks, administration officials have instead intensified an economic isolation campaign, during which the US has threatened to slap countries that trade with Iran with massive sanctions, while maintaining its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.
The trade-focused strategy, however, has its own limits, analysts and officials said.
Iran has spent decades under layers of US and international sanctions that have battered its economy but have not deterred its leadership.
On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the pressure campaign may cause Iran to lash out militarily, raising the prospect that the economic campaign could itself stoke military escalation.
Additionally, some major world powers, like China, have not joined Washington's bid to isolate Iran, prompting questions about the campaign's effectiveness.
"The purpose of the new sanctions package is meant to add economic pressure on top of that being caused by the blockade to force Iran back to the table, after the administration determined it was a better option than returning to kinetic action," said Alex Plitsas, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council.
"Iran is concerned about it, but China has already indicated that it's not willing to play ball, which calls into question how effective it will be."

articles.title: Germany successfully tests Israeli ballistic missile
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Germany successfully tests Israeli ballistic missile, officials say
Germany successfully tested an Israeli ballistic missile in the North Atlantic overnight, military officials said on Wednesday, as Western powers scramble to acquire long-range weapons to counter what they see as an increased threat from Russia.
The test of what officials said was a LORA missile built by Israel Aerospace Industries came hours after Berlin publicly blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month and ordered measures in response.
Germany does not currently have ballistic missiles, which fly at much higher speeds than the cruise missiles in its arsenal. The Israeli-built system has a range of up to 500 km (310 miles), Germany's defence ministry said.
Berlin is engaged in a number of multinational collaborations aimed at developing long-range missiles, and also looking at options to buy such weapons.
Navy chief Jan Christian Kaack said the test was a success.
"Our units can successfully deploy the system, and its potential range exceeds anything we have seen before," he said in a statement. "In terms of protecting Germany and our allies, this test marks a new chapter in deterrence and maritime defence readiness."
Germany is also working on an upgraded version of its Taurus cruise missile, currently its only weapon with a range of several hundred kilometres, with production scheduled to start in 2029.
The upgraded Taurus NEO missile will feature an extended range, improved shielding against interference, and advancements in navigation and seeker head technology, according to a budget document.
German forces have about 600 Taurus missiles with an official range of more than 500 km (310 miles) in their inventories, that can be launched from fighter jets such as the Tornado, the F-15 or the F-18.
The weapon, built by European defence company MBDA, is designed to destroy targets behind enemy lines such as command bunkers, ammunition and fuel dumps, airfields and bridges.

articles.title: Iran attacks US bases in Middle East after reports of fatal strike on wedding – Middle East crisis live
articles.body:
Trump suggests strait of Hormuz could be renamed 'Trump strait'
US president Donald Trump has suggested renaming the strait of Hormuz ‘Trump strait’.
In a post on his Truth Social network, he wrote:
Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT??? Like America itself, it would be “hotter” than ever before!
Trump has in recent weeks repeatedly pressed a threat to claim sovereignty over the strait of Hormuz, even posting a map showing the waterway as a “new US territory.”
Donald Trump said that while the US is prepared to attack Iran again “any time we want”,he doesn’t think the renewed campaign against Iran would last “too long”. He also declined to comment on how serious he was about wanting to rename the strait of Hormuz after himself.
The Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, accused the US of committing a war crime following a reported deadly strike that hit a wedding party in southern Iran, killing at least four people, including a four-year-old child, and injuring 68 others.
Washington has still made no official comment on the attack. A spokesperson for US Central Command, Tim Hawkins, said the US was aware of reports of civilian casualties, but said the “US military never targets civilians”. He told the Associated Press the US military was looking into the reports of the strike on a wedding, but would not say if the military had launched a formal investigation.
The Iranian Red Crescent has written to the international criminal court (ICC) calling for legal action to be taken against the USfollowing the attack, which is said could constitute a war crime. In the letter, the Iranian Red Crescent said: “Given the reported civilian character of the location as the venue of a family wedding ceremony, as well as the presence of civilians at the site, the incident raises serious concerns under international humanitarian law and warrants an independent, impartial, thorough, and effective investigation.” It added: “Should an independent investigation establish that the wedding venue and the persons present therein were of a civilian character, that no lawful military objective was present at the location, or that the attack was carried out without due regard for the requirements of distinction, proportionality, and precautions in attack, the incident may constitute a serious violation of international humanitarian law and, where the requisite elements are established, a war crime.”
Meanwhile, Benjamin Netanyahu has said that Israel’s mission in Iran is “not yet finished”. “All of our systems under my direction are working to overthrow this regime,” the Israeli prime minister told i24News’s Hebrew channel. “Our pilots were there and they can be there at at any moment. We have not yet finished the job. We can be there at any moment. We will defeat this regime.”Asked what defeat meant, Netanyahu said: “We will bring it down. It’s already on its last legs anyway.”
Earlier, his defence minister, Israel Katz, had said the IDF is ready to respond “with great force” if Iran attacks Israel, amid the renewed fighting between the United States and Iran. And his foreign minister, Gideon Saar, echoed Katz’s remarks in an interview with the broadcaster France 24 that aired on Wednesday. “If we will be attacked by Iran, we will surely respond heavily, but I’m not sure that Iran will do that mistake,” Saar said. “We don’t have the plans to join the war right now.”
And Iran’s currency, the rial, hit a record low on Wednesday. Traders in the Tehran market exchanged 2.20 million rials for one US dollar. That was nearly 10% higher than last week’s record, set on 25 August, when one dollar was sold at 2.02 million rials. The rial has repeatedly hit new lows since the US and Israel launched the conflict more than six months ago. It has lost about half of its value in a year of tightening US sanctions and American and Israeli attacks.
Earlier, we reported that the Israeli defence minister, Israel Katz, had said his military is ready to respond “with great force” if Iran attacks Israel, amid renewed fighting between the United States and Iran.
Speaking at a conference hosted by the Israeli news outlet Ynet, Katz said:
We do not want to be caught off guard; we are prepared. It must be understood: the IDF [Israel Defense Forces], including the air force, is prepared to strike in Iran.
If they attack us, we will respond with great force, without relying on anyone.
Since launching the war on Iran alongside the United States in late February, Israel has largely stayed on the sidelines of recent clashes between the US and Iran.
The Israeli foreign minister, Gideon Saar, said that would likely remain the case, while echoing Katz’s remarks in an interview with the broadcaster France 24 that aired on Wednesday.
If we will be attacked by Iran, we will surely respond heavily, but I’m not sure that Iran will do that mistake.
We don’t have the plans to join the war right now.
Iran retaliates after US strikes reportedly kill wedding guests - podcast
Iran has accused the United States of a “war crime” after a missile blast killed at least four people, including a young child, and injured 68 at a wedding at a private house in southern Iran.
A month-long uneasy truce between the US and Iran appears to have collapsed again, after US strikes on Saturday on Larak Island in the strait of Hormuz. Iran has responded by launching drones and missiles on US bases across the Middle East, including the Gulf States.
In today’s edition of The Latest podcast, Lucy Hough speaks to Middle East correspondent Will Christou. Also available on YouTube.
The funeral for those who were killed in the US strike on a wedding ceremony in Kuhestak in southern Iran on Tuesday night is scheduled to take place on Thursday, according to the Fars news agency, citing the IRGC public relations office in Hormozgan province.
The state news agency IRNA and state TV said two women and two children, aged 4 and 16, were killed, and at least 68 were wounded when a US missile hit a home where dozens were gathered to celebrate the wedding of a fisherman’s daughter.
US Central Command spokesman Captain Tim Hawkins told the Associated Press the US military was looking into the reports of the strike on a wedding. He would not say if the military had launched a formal investigation.
Trump also told reporters that he had brought up the issue of price gouging in a meeting with oil and gas executives on Tuesday, adding that he wanted retail gasoline prices to come down.
It is worth noting that as Trump touts last night’s “heavy attack”, Washington has still made no official comment after at least four people were killed and 68 injured after shrapnel from a US missile reportedly hit a home where a wedding was being held in Sirik, southern Iran.
The Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, has accused the US of committing a war crime. The Associated Press reported earlier the US military said it was aware of the allegations but that it “never targets civilians”.
Trump says US prepared to attack Iran again 'any time we want'
Trump also claimed that Iran was trying to rebuild radar and missile systems, along with a rocket that drops mines. “We took it out,” he told reporters in the Oval Office.
“We hit them last night because they took a shot at our base in Jordan,” he went on. “We hit them hard last night. They gave a little love-tap, but we hit them hard.”
He said the US military had “taken out” the new equipment that Iran was building along the strait of Hormuz, “some defensive, some offensive.”
The US president added:
We blew up much more than their radar last night, it was a very heavy attack last night. And we’re prepared to do another one any time we want.
Trump says renewed US campaign against Iran won't last long
Asked how long his renewed campaign against Iran might go on for, Trump replied briefly: “I don’t think too long.”
He also said of oil prices, which went up again to $95 a barrel: “They’ll come down.”
And given his claims about “decimating” Iran’s military, he was asked what is left to strike and why?
Trump didn’t answer directly, instead claiming that the United States has “very strong control” of the strait of Hormuz.
We are controlling the Hormuz strait, we are bringing lots of boats out everyday with millions of barrels of oil.
We are for the most part doing it without trouble, every once in a while they shoot a drone and we knock it down. We have control, very strong control.
Speaking of Donald Trump, he’s currently speaking to reporters in the Oval Office as he meets with US travel executives. He’ll likely be asked about Iran and I’ll bring you all the relevant lines here.
Donald Trump’s suggestion of renaming the strait of Hormuz after himself – which he has no authority to do – has prompted criticism from US Democrats.
“No need for more renaming bodies of water here. Americans already call this entire fiasco TRUMP’S WAR,” Senate minority leader Chuck Schumersaid on X. “Trump cares more about feeding his ego than helping the American people who are crying out for help. They want lower health care costs, lower gas prices and grocery bills, and for our troops to come home.”
Schumer’s post included a link to Trump’s Truth Social missive from earlier today where he said: “Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT???”
Trump also said: “Like America itself, it would be ‘hotter’ than ever before!”
It comes after his efforts to rename the Gulf of Mexico and LakeOntario to the Gulf of America and Lake America, respectively.
Iran has blacklisted more ships from sailing through the Strait of Hormuz.
According to reporting by Reuters, Tehran has deemed another 11 ships to be non-compliant with rules it has imposed on using the major shipping passage. Iranian authorities said the listed vessels could be subject to fines, confiscation or detention if they attempt to pass through the strait.
The update was made via the website of the Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA), a body set up by Iran to manage the strait, increasing the total number of blacklisted vessels to 56.
The restrictions are likely to further constrain efforts to export oil via the strait, which before the war handled about 20% of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments but has since seen traffic reduced mostly to a trickle.

articles.title: Berlin’s latest Russia panic is reckless even by its own standards
articles.body:
Berlin’s latest Russia panic is reckless even by its own standards
When you’ve burned all your bridges, go and burn some more.
That seems to be the unspoken strategy of Berlin’s policy toward Moscow, which is the only plausible interpretation of Germany’s fresh efforts to damage its already abysmal relationship with Russia. Not that they have come as a surprise. Since the odd drone incident at the Leipzig/Halle airport at the beginning of August, the German political establishment and its always compliant mainstream media have been preparing the ground for explicitly blaming Moscow.
The German public has been subject to what looks like a systematic campaign of escalating innuendo for almost a month. The story emerging from this barrage of unfounded claims and speculation masquerading as self-evident certainty has been changing: the role of an airport bus driver merely discovering the drone sitting quietly on the tarmac next to an extra-large Ukrainian transport plane or kicking it to the ground with a Bruce-Lee-type flying kick, as initially claimed, has remained unclear and contradictory. Initial reports of another drone colliding with a plane in flight had to be retracted when traces of birds became too obvious.
Now, clearly, the time has come to make things official. The German government, represented by Minister of the Interior Alexander Dobrindt and foreign policy chief Johann Wadephul, has blamed the drone incident on Russian intelligence services and announced retaliation measures, such as closing a consulate and cultural center in Berlin, even more travel restrictions and individual sanctions on Russians, and fresh attempts to go after Russian ships by, in effect, piracy. The Russian ambassador has been called in, various EU governments, the EU commission, and NATO – though not the US – have made a grand show out of supporting Germany.
Moscow has roundly rejected Berlin’s accusations, called in the German chargé d’affaires, and promised a symmetric response to Germany’s actions. President Vladimir Putin has plausibly described them as a “grave mistake” and, equally plausibly, surmised that it is due mainly to attempts to shape elections and distract from Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s historically sensational unpopularity.
So far, so bad: Berlin has managed to reach a new low-point in a relationship that is crucial for Germany but which it loves to tear apart. As Sarah Wagenknecht of the new-left BSW party has noted, the drone did not do any damage, regardless of the question of where it came from. The German government, though, has deliberately chosen a massive over-reaction. The new-right AfD’s Ulrich Siegmund, likely to soon make history by winning the AfD’s first state elections, has also called for moderation and dialogue instead of escalation. In today’s Germany, reason is literally on the political margins, while the self-declared Center has gone nuts.
What is even worse, however, is that no proof has been presented of Russian involvement. It is true that after the announcement of Berlin’s official blame game, conveniently timed leaks to the mainstream media have conveyed unsubstantiated claims about two holders of Russian passports being involved. But this conspicuous combination of a specific accusation presented without evidence and clearly coordinated leaks merely hinting at it makes the impression of manipulation even worse.
Not to speak of the fact that these passports – if they exist and if they actually belong to real perpetrators – are extremely flimsy and, frankly, bizarre pieces of evidence: Why would Russian intelligence services make sure their agents carry Russian passports? If anyone had an interest in making it that easy to point fingers at Moscow it would surely be either Ukraine, which has a vile record in terrorist false flag operations, lying, and subterfuge of the worst sort. For Kiev, it would have been ideal to place a drone that creates hysteria in Berlin but fails to destroy an asset as valuable and rare as the AN-124 Condor transport aircraft.
The fact that the West in general and Germany in particular already has a long record of proven false alarms about Russian drones has also made no difference. As the Germans say, where there’s a will, there’s a way. And the will to deepen tensions with Russia is boundless among the current German establishment.
Speaking of which, it is impossible not to be stunned by the difference between Berlin’s treatment of a devastating terror attack which did actually work and one that either failed or was staged to begin with: We now know that Ukraine – most likely with the help of one or more NATO states – committed the 2022 Nord Stream pipeline attack, that is the single worst sabotage of postwar Germany’s vital infrastructure, economy, and environment while blaming Russia.
Yet Berlin has shown a consistent pattern of tolerating or even helping with the cover-up, while going as slow as possible on investigation and prosecution, while Ukraine’s leader Vladimir Zelensky keeps boldly lying. That is the state of the art almost four years after the attack. That and a relentless and unceasing flow of gazillions of German taxpayers’ money to the Kiev perpetrator regime. So much for “not rewarding the aggressor”: National masochism is too kind a term.
After the Leipzig/Halle incident it has taken less than a month to come to sweeping conclusions and reach for strong retaliatory measures while not presenting evidence. What a contrast. Clearly, those commentators are right who guess that Berlin’s newfound capacity for rapid over-reaction is rooted in several aggressive policy agendas: the current push to turn the German foreign intelligence service BND into an instrument of sabotage paramilitary operations; the new militarism which aims to build the most powerful conventional army in Europe and is explicitly targeting Moscow, and, last but not least, turning hatred and fear of Russia into a distraction in a country in deep economic crisis.
If Berlin is not preparing for open war with Russia, it is certainly doing its best to leave precisely that impression. Many Germans do not agree with this road-to-perdition course. For all of Europe’s sake, let’s hope that they will finally manage to change it.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

articles.title: Russia secretly aiding Iran in development of supersonic cruise missile technology - report
articles.body:
Russia has been secretly helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles, London-based outlet The Financial Times reported on Wednesday morning, which experts say would likely have been intended for anti-ship and land attacks.
The program, codenamed C430L, began in 2023 and was arranged by Russia's state arms exporter, Rosoboronexport, in coordination with the US-sanctioned NPO Mashinostroyenia, FT reported.
According to FT, Russian arms export officials and senior NPO Mashinostroyenia engineers traveled to Iran repeatedly in 2023.
Among the engineers who conducted these trips were Alexander Dergachev, chief designer for sea-launched missiles and cruise missile complexes; Alexander Chebakov, head of NPO Mashinostroyenia’s design department for air-breathing propulsion units and a specialist in supersonic ramjet propulsion for cruise missiles; and Yuri Prokhorchuk, head of the aerodynamics and ballistics department.
FT also learned that Vladislav Kuzmichev, head of Rosoboronexport’s department of defense technologies and space, accompanied the delegation on its third trip to Iran, and later negotiated the C430L contract with Iran.
By 2025, NPO Mashinostroyenia had received various Iranian technical materials, which Russian engineers analyzed and responded to with various questions.
In correspondence seen by FT from April 2025, Rosoboronexport proposed sending a delegation of Russian specialists to Iran and asked Tehran to answer the engineers' questions before the trip.
“People often think about technology transfers as being solely about sending blueprints, parts, or entire missiles," Fabian Hinz, an Iranian missiles expert and senior analyst with Conflict Armament Research, a UK-based weapons-tracing organization, told FT, "but getting a 60-year-old engineer to fly over and problem-solve, using their experience, is hugely valuable.”
Iranian president thanks Putin for support against United States
On Tuesday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for Moscow's position on the war in Iran and resulting sanctions, and said that together, Moscow and Tehran can resist what he called US "unilateralism."
The two leaders spoke on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek.
During the meeting, Putin told Pezeshkian that Moscow stood in solidarity with the Iranian people in the fight for their interests.
Putin also said that Russia and Iran will maintain their economic and trade relationship despite the current military and political environment.
“During this difficult period, we are striving to provide you with the necessary assistance - as we have discussed - and are supplying you with essential goods,” Putin said.
Pezeshkian accuses US of violating international law
Pezeshkian, in turn, said that the US does not have the right to impose sanctions "whenever they please," and accused them of violating international law and committing acts of aggression.
Russia and Iran, he said, would find ways to circumvent the US sanctions.
"Within frameworks like the SCO and other organizations, we can bypass unilateral measures and cooperate on a multilateral basis,” he stated.
Notably, the US sanctions Pezeshkian was referring to, including Washington’s latest measures targeting Iranian financial networks and IRGC-linked assets, are not in themselves prohibited under international law. Economic sanctions also do not constitute an “act of aggression” under the UN definition.
Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Ukraine urges UN aviation agency to fully ban operations in Russian airspace
articles.body:
Ukraine warns Russian airspace ‘not safe’ in message to UN aviation watchdog
Ukraine urged the UN aviation agency to call for a full ban on flights through Russian airspace, after President Volodymyr Zelensky warned it was becoming unsafe. Kyiv plans increased retaliation against intensified Russian strikes but would target only military facilities, Zelensky said, citing growing Ukrainian drone activity over Russia.
Ukraine has urged the UN's aviation agency to ask its members to fully ban operations in Russian airspace, a day after President Volodymyr Zelensky warned it was "becoming completely unsafe".
On Tuesday, top Ukrainian officials said the country would step up retaliation against Russia's intensified strikes on Kyiv, which has been under continuous air raid alerts for seven days and has suffered hits on civilian infrastructure.
Ukraine would only target Russian military facilities and not threaten civilian aircraft, Zelensky added, but he stressed that the growing number of Ukrainian drones in Russian skies should "be taken into account".
In a letter to International Civil Aviation Organisation Chairman Juan Carlos Salazar, a copy of which was exclusively shared with Reuters, Ukraine's Infrastructure Minister Mykola Kalashnyk said Kyiv believed the risk of tragedies in the skies should be minimised.
Ukraine asked ICAO to encourage aviation authorities and airlines to safeguard civil aviation, "including by facilitating the full prohibition by ICAO member states of civil aircraft operations within the airspace of the Russian Federation".
While European and US carriers do not fly over Russia due to the war that erupted when Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the airspace is used by airlines from countries such as China, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf states.
