ICAO cannot impose rules on its 193 member countries, but its decisions influence national policies. The Montreal-based UN agency uses consensus to set standards on everything from runways to seat belts.
While not mentioning any specific country, ICAO on Wednesday warned in a statement that the risk of weapons targeting commercial planes is growing and called for stronger commitments from countries to protect aircraft from conflict zone risks.
"ICAO is observing heightened risks of civil aircraft being targeted or caught in crossfire," the statement said. "While the aviation industry is able to reroute flights and maintain operations during conflicts, this operational flexibility does not address the fundamental security threat."
Aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions said in an analysis that Ukraine's drone and missile attacks have already demonstrated their reach deep into Russia, leading to airport closures and flight cancellations.
"Zelensky is articulating publicly what Ukraine has been doing for months: systematically disrupting Russian airspace," Osprey said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said Zelenskiy's comments amounted to "state terrorism". Moscow on Wednesday vowed to head off any disruption to civil aviation.
In 2024, 38 people were killed when an Azerbaijan Airlines plane heading to Russia's Grozny crash-landed in Kazakhstan after diverting from its course. Putin later said two Russian missiles detonated near the aircraft after Ukrainian drones entered the airspace.
Ukraine closed its airspace to civilian traffic when Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, unleashing missile barrages without issuing warnings to civilian aircraft in Ukrainian airspace.
Airports have remained closed ever since, and SkyUp, Ukraine's only surviving airline, now operates from neighbouring Moldova.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

articles.title: They came for a wedding dance, Trump gave them the dance of death
articles.body:
They came for a wedding dance, Trump gave them the dance of death
TEHRAN – A fresh wave of deadly missile strikes carried out by United States military forces against civilian infrastructure and residential gatherings across southern Iran on Tuesday night has left over a dozen people dead and scores of others wounded, triggering widespread outrage and renewed calls for international criminal accountability over blatant violations of international humanitarian law.
The overnight aggression struck three separate locations in the vicinity of Ahvaz and Aghajari in the southwestern province of Khuzestan, alongside a series of lethal bombardments across the southern coastal province of Hormozgan.
The most egregious atrocity occurred in the coastal town of Kouhestak, situated in Hormozgan’s Sirik County, where American ordnance struck an active family wedding ceremony at around 8:00 p.m. local time on Tuesday. The horrific blast turned a peaceful gathering into a scene of carnage, killing at least five civilians and severely injuring 68 others, with women and children making up a large share of the casualties. Local medical personnel confirmed that a four-year-old child was among those killed on the spot.
Following the massacre, the United States Central Command (CENTCOM) issued an official statement attempting to justify the fatal strikes, falsely claiming that American forces had launched attacks exclusively on targets belonging to Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC). CENTCOM attempted to link the aggression to what Washington described as recent Iranian actions against commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and alleged security threats to US forces stationed in the region.
Provincial officials and local witnesses vehemently dismissed Washington’s narrative, stressing that the struck site in Kouhestak was a clearly identifiable residential and social venue hosting a traditional family wedding reception with hundreds of non-combatants present.
The devastating strike on the Kouhestak wedding has drawn swift and unequivocal condemnation from legal observers, human rights defenders, and Iranian humanitarian bodies. In an official letter submitted to the International Criminal Court (ICC), the Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) demanded immediate legal action and a formal investigation following the US missile attack on the ceremony.
In its statement, the IRCS emphasized that given the reported civilian character of the location as the venue of a family wedding ceremony, as well as the presence of civilians at the site, the incident raises serious concerns under international humanitarian law and warrants an independent, impartial, thorough, and effective investigation.
The IRCS underscored that the Kouhestak massacre, which left innocent families devastated, constitutes a clear war crime under all established legal frameworks.
Senior Iranian officials have reacted with sharp indignation to the latest wave of American aerial assaults. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf forcefully condemned the attack on the wedding ceremony, stating that the deliberate targeting of civilians at schools, sports complexes, and social gatherings shows that Washington is operating and killing “like Satan.”
In a post on social platform X on Wednesday, Qalibaf stated that the Kouhestak bombing represents an indivisible part of a sustained campaign against defenseless civilians, referencing earlier high-casualty strikes against an educational center in Minab and a sports facility in Lamerd. He wrote: “Minab school: children massacred. Lamerd sports hall: kids slaughtered. Kouhestak wedding: children killed with families. If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan, and kills like Satan, it’s Satan. Shields a junior Satan that does the same? It’s THE Great Satan.”
Hassan Ghashghavi, spokesman for the Iranian Parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, also questioned how the United States military could claim advanced reconnaissance capabilities while repeatedly hitting soft civilian targets. Ghashghavi stated that a regime which claims to utilize comprehensive satellite coverage to monitor even the smallest movement on Earth cannot credibly claim it failed to distinguish military installations from a school, a sports venue, or a wedding ceremony. He added that the United States has for decades dropped bombs and missiles on defenseless populations while routinely leaving the justification of its crimes to post-facto inquiry committees.
The latest strikes on Khuzestan and Hormozgan are part of an intensifying military confrontation that began on February 28, when joint military escalation by the United States and Israel plunged the region into active hostilities. During 39 days of war, Washington and Tel Aviv carried out repeated air and missile incursions across Iran, resulting in widespread civilian bloodshed that contradicts Western claims of precision targeting. A Pakistani-mediated memorandum of understanding reached between the US and Iran on June 17—designed to underpin the ceasefire that had paused hostilities since April 8—was violated by the administration of President Donald Trump.
The tragedy in Kouhestak follows earlier high-casualty attacks that shocked the nation. On the first day of the war on February 28, a catastrophic US strike hit a school in the city of Minab in Hormozgan province during peak school hours, killing 168 people, the vast majority of whom were young school children attending class alongside their teachers and school staff. The horrific loss of 168 lives in Minab triggered instantaneous global outrage, prompting protests across international capitals, emergency statements from international legal bodies, and direct condemnations from human rights watchdogs that denounced the carnage as a flagrant breach of the Geneva Conventions and international legal protections afforded to educational facilities.
That tragedy was compounded shortly afterward in Lamerd, Fars Province, where an aerial strike blasted a community sports hall during scheduled youth sports training sessions. The attack in Lamerd killed young athletes, coaches, and spectators, critically wounding scores more and reducing a vital public recreation center to rubble.
The deliberate bombing of the Minab school, the Lamerd sports hall, and now the Kouhestak wedding ceremony underscores a continuous and documented pattern of attacks on protected civilian sites. Legal experts note that the sheer scale of non-combatant casualties across Minab, Lamerd, and Kouhestak dismantles any pretense of collateral damage and demonstrates systemic negligence and criminal disregard for human life.
Shortly following the latest aggression in Khuzestan and Hormozgan, Iran’s Armed Forces responded by staging a series of combined retaliatory operations featuring precision ballistic and cruise missile strikes alongside advanced long-range drone barrages targeting regional American military installations and strategic interests.
Iranian military and diplomatic officials have reiterated that the Islamic Republic will exercise its legitimate right to self-defense under Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, affirming that unprovoked aggression against Iranian soil, citizens, and civilian infrastructure will be met with decisive responses and relentless pursuit of justice through international legal tribunals.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says airlines should avoid Russian airspace as Ukraine expands drone operations
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged airlines to avoid Russian airspace as Kyiv expands its drone operations.
"We want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia's key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe," Zelenskyy said Tuesday in his evening address.
His warning follows Ukraine stepping up its long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries and logistics hubs, as it seeks to raise the cost of the war for Moscow.
Ukraine's president said it is important that airlines currently flying into airports in Moscow, St. Petersburg and other key destinations in Russia take note of the elevated airspace risk.
Zelenskyy insisted that civilian aviation would not be in danger, before adding: "There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account."
Most Western commercial airlines do not fly into Russian airspace due to Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Some Chinese and Gulf state carriers, including Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, continue to use Russian airspace, however.
In response to Zelenskyy's comments, Russian President Vladimir Putin said the threat amounted to a declaration of "state terrorism." He added that the Kremlin would continue intensifying its own attacks on Ukraine.
Speaking to reporters at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan on Tuesday, Putin also dismissed the idea of resuming negotiations, saying: "You don't negotiate with terrorists."
'Massive strikes'
Ukraine closed its airspace to civilian aircraft after Russia launched its full-scale invasion.
"The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine and our other institutions will provide international organizations with full information about the dangers in Russian airspace. Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation," Zelenskyy said.
Earlier in the week, Russia's Defense Ministry said it is planning "massive strikes" on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, amplifying fears of another winter assault.
Russian forces have ramped up missile strikes on Ukrainian cities as Kyiv faces a shortage of air defense equipment.

articles.title: Iran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills four people at wedding
articles.body:
Iran has accused the US of a war crime after a missile blast killed at least four people and injured 68 who were attending a wedding at a private home in a coastal city of southern Iran, as the fresh exchange of strikes prompted fears of a wider renewal of hostilities.
Iranian media said that the wedding ceremony was being held in a home in the city of Kuhestak, Hormozgan province, late on Tuesday when a US missile struck, with shrapnel and debris from the strike killing and injuring people.
Among the dead was a four-year-old child, Amir-Ali Karimi, and a 16-year-old, Mohammad Mollahi.
“It’s a terrible thing. I’m extremely worried and upset about what happened – really upset,” Ali Mollahi, the father of the bride, told Mehr News.
A video of the aftermath shows colourful wedding streamers and decorations strewn across the ground, and shoes abandoned in the rush to escape the attack.
“You wicked people have attacked people’s homes and turned their wedding ceremony into a funeral,” said a man filming the aftermath of the strike, shared by Fars news agency.
The deputy of the provincial government, Ahmad Nafisi, said first responders had headed immediately to the scene and transferred the wounded to the hospitals.
Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson called the US attack a “war crime” and said Iran “will respond to these savage crimes with firmness”.
The chief Iranian negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, said the attack had killed families with children, and called the US the “great Satan”.
“If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan and kills like Satan, it’s Satan. Shields a junior Satan that does the same? It’s THE Great Satan,” Ghalibaf said in a post on X.
The US attacks followed strikes on Sunday, ending a month-long uneasy truce between the US and Iran, and appeared to signal a resumption of another cycle of escalation. US Central Command (Centcom) said the overnight strikes focused on Iranian military targets, including air defence sites, radars and maritime assets.
Iran responded by launching drones and missiles on US bases across the Middle East, including in Bahrain, Kuwait and the UAE. Iran’s military spokesperson, Lt Col Ebrahim Zolfaghari, vowed “heavier, broader, and more crushing and devastating” retaliation.
Videos of the aftermath of the strike show a caved-in roof, blown-out windows and ground riddled with debris, as well as walls pockmarked with what appeared to be holes from shrapnel. Footage from a nearby hospital showed women in wedding attire watching as injured children were being treated.
“When we arrived there, an explosion occurred. It was very intense. Bricks, stones and cement hit me in the face and head, and many others were injured,” a child who was injured at the wedding told the state-affiliated Fars news agency.
A woman with her hands decorated in henna for the nuptials posted a video on Instagram after the attack, saying “my hands and feet are still shaking”.
A spokesperson for Centcom, Tim Hawkins, said the US was aware of reports of civilian casualties, but the “US military never targets civilians, unlike the [Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps]”.
In February, a strike on an elementary school killed at least 156 people, including more than 120 schoolchildren. Independent investigations concluded that the US likely carried out the strike with the assistance of AI, though the US government said the incident remained under investigation.
Pictures of shrapnel collected at the site of Tuesday’s attack were published on Iranian state media, and appeared to show the internal components of US munitions. Trevor Ball, an independent weapons analyst, identified some of the remnants as belonging to the Standoff Land Attack Missile-Expanded Response (Slam-Er) missile, which is made by the US weapons company Boeing. The Slam-Er is a 1,500-pound, GPS-guided missile touted by Boeing to be “extremely accurate”.
It was unclear if the home where the wedding was being held was struck directly, or if a missile hit close to the home and debris from the strike hit the home and its occupants. CCTV footage captured at least six strikes in the area within a minute. A separate strike appeared to hit a communications tower about 150 metres away from the home.
Authorities said that several “telecommunications and internet towers and sites were also seriously damaged in the latest strikes”.
The US has been targeting communications and radar infrastructure along Iran’s coast to try to stop its blockade on the strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint which prior to the US-Iran war was a transit point for at least 20% of the world’s oil supply.
Iran has virtually closed the strait since the start of the Iran war, frustrating the US president, Donald Trump, who is facing a midterm election with expensive gas prices and knock-on inflation across the board.
In recent weeks, the US has focused on trying to degrade Iran’s capacity to strike ships transiting the strait to reopen the waterway for traffic.

articles.title: Zelensky Demands Accountability Following ‘Absolutely Disgraceful’ SBU-HUR Shootout in Kyiv
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky has ordered a full investigation and demanded accountability following a shootout in Kyiv between the personnel of Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR).
In a statement issued on Wednesday, Sept. 2, Zelensky said that he had spoken with Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko. The Prosecutor General’s Office and the State Bureau of Investigation (DBR) will examine testimony and statements from all individuals linked to the shootout, reconstructing the events step by step.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“There must be accountability, including personnel decisions by the heads of the special services regarding those involved in what happened,” Zelensky said.
“Internal investigations must also be conducted within both services,” he continued.
What is known
The shooting occurred on Yuriya Shumskoho Street in Kyiv’s Dniprovskyi district on Wednesday morning. Authorities later blocked the area as investigators examined the incident.
The Prosecutor General’s Office said SBU officers had been carrying out actions intended to prevent an unspecified terrorist act allegedly prepared by Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB).
During the search, an armed group allegedly fired at the SBU’s operational-investigative team, obstructed the officers’ passage with vehicles and attempted to stop the investigation.
Ukraine Seeks Billions From EU for Patriot Missiles
The prosecutor’s office said the SBU’s special Alpha unit was deployed, with the attackers later detained. It described them as members of one of Ukraine’s Defense Forces units, while media reports identified the personnel involved as belonging to HUR.
Three HUR personnel were reportedly injured during the confrontation.
Possible link to RDK
Several Ukrainian media outlets, including Ukrainska Pravda, reported that the incident may be connected to the disappearance of Stepan Kaplunov, deputy commander of the Russian Volunteer Corps (RDK) – a unit made up of Russian nationals fighting for Ukraine against Moscow.
Earlier on Wednesday morning, the SBU said it had worked with HUR to thwart an attack prepared by Russia’s FSB against a Russian opposition leader who had arrived in Ukraine for Independence Day. However, neither agency publicly identified the intended target or confirmed that it was indeed Kaplunov.
Meanwhile, the RDK reportedly said Kaplunov had disappeared near his home several days earlier and that it had reported his disappearance to Ukrainian law enforcement bodies, including the SBU and HUR.
Ukrainska Pravda separately reported that Kaplunov’s lawyer, Taras Borovskyi, said the serviceman had been released, though his whereabouts remain unknown.
Investigation and accountability
Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Presidential Office and former HUR chief, called for a thorough investigation.
“It is important to ensure a thorough and impartial investigation, but no one has the right to kidnap servicemen with impunity, open fire on the streets of our cities, give and carry out criminal orders,” Budanov told RBC-Ukraine.
Additionally, Zelensky signed a decree dismissing Oleh Khramov – head of the SBU’s Department for State Secrets Protection and Licensing, according to Ukrainska Pravda.

articles.title: How Iran disabled the largest US naval base in West Asia
articles.body:
How Iran disabled the largest US naval base in West Asia
TEHRAN — The strategic architecture of the Persian Gulf underwent a seismic realignment with the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran that began on February 28. In a rapid and calculated operational response to the aggression, the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran executed precision retaliatory strikes against key military hubs across the region, dealing a severe and crippling blow to Washington’s forward-deployed infrastructure.
At the very center of this collapse is Naval Support Activity (NSA) Bahrain, the largest and most critical US naval installation in West Asia. For decades, the sprawling facility served as the operational headquarters for the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet and the primary command-and-control node for American naval hegemony across the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, the Arabian Sea, and the Red Sea. Constructed and expanded to project American power directly onto Iran’s doorstep, the base housed thousands of military personnel, advanced command centers, logistical stockpiles, and deep-water berthing infrastructure. It was treated by the Pentagon as an untouchable fortress capable of sustaining carrier strike groups, guided-missile destroyers, and amphibious ready groups indefinitely.
However, when the US-Israeli war on Iran commenced on February 28, Iran’s targeted missile and drone salvos shattered that assumption within the opening hours of the conflict. By striking critical command facilities, logistical depots, and support infrastructure at NSA Bahrain, Iran effectively neutralized the base’s ability to function as a forward headquarters. The strike stripped the US Navy of its secure onshore rear-echelon support, forcing an immediate evacuation of personnel and cutting off the Fifth Fleet from its primary logistical lifeline in the region.
The lingering consequences of this operational setback were brought into sharp relief during a recent worldwide town hall held by the US Navy’s top brass, including Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle and Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy John Perryman. Speaking before an audience of sailors at Fort Meade, Maryland, and connected remotely to personnel worldwide, Caudle faced direct questions regarding the ongoing crisis resulting from the strikes.
The first question of the day came from a seaman who asked about household goods displaced by an Iranian attack on Bahrain at the start of the war with Iran. Caudle said a return to the base was not imminent.
“We’re not getting back in there anytime soon,” he said. “I just want to be completely honest with that. But we’re working real hard to develop a scheme of maneuver in order for you to get your things.”
This direct statement from the Chief of Naval Operations serves as official recognition of the operational void created by Iran’s defensive strikes. Rather than discussing force projection or operational readiness out of Manama, the Navy’s highest-ranking admiral was reduced to addressing how displaced sailors might eventually retrieve their abandoned household goods through a scheme of maneuver.
The disabling of NSA Bahrain has triggered a domino effect across US naval operations throughout the theater. Stripped of their primary port of call and sustainment facilities, US carrier strike groups have faced unprecedented operational friction. Deployments have stretched past 250 days without standard port calls, causing acute supply deficits in basic food and hygiene goods, compounding maintenance backlogs, and eroding crew morale and readiness. Furthermore, the loss of secure basing in Bahrain has forced the Pentagon into chaotic asset reshuffling, including deploying the USS Theodore Roosevelt to the Arabian Sea to relieve the USS George Washington.
Ultimately, the neutralization of NSA Bahrain proves that forward US bases, long utilized to encircle and intimidate sovereign regional states, have turned into acute tactical liabilities under the precision envelope of Iranian deterrence. By knocking the largest US naval installation in West Asia offline from the earliest days of the war, Iran demonstrated that the era of uncontested American military footprint in regional waters has effectively come to an end.

articles.title: US and Iran Trade Strikes as Fighting Resumes in Gulf
articles.body:
U.S. Central Command launched a wave of strikes against Iran on Sept. 1, and President Donald Trump said forces are “prepared to do another one” as Iran launched retaliatory attacks Sept. 2.
Fighting resumed Aug. 30, as CENTCOM officials announced strikes on “minelaying forces posing an imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz.” Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has been using land-based launchers to lob floating mines into the Strait.
Speaking in the Oval Office on Sept. 2, Trump said he ended the roughly monthlong pause in hostilities because of sea mines.
“They were trying to rebuild their radar systems and a missile system and … to build a rocket that drops mines,” Trump said at a White House event. “They were building it, it was almost finished, so we took it out. We saw that they were building it, we see everything that they’re doing.”
Iranian forces countered with ballistic missile attacks on U.S. forces in Jordan and on civilian ships transiting the Strait. A number of U.S. Air Force personnel and assets are stationed at the base in Jordan that has previously come under attack.
On Sept. 1, CENTCOM announced additional strikes on IRGC targets in retaliation for “attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region.” The command indicated its targets included “air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine-laying capabilities, and communications sites.”
Trump called the U.S. strikes “a very heavy attack” that “took out all of the new equipment that they tried to build along the Strait of Hormuz: some defensive, some offensive.”
Iranian state media outlets alleged the strikes also hit a wedding party in a coastal town, but those claims remain unconfirmed.
Iranian forces launched their latest retaliatory strikes Sept. 2. Officials and media outlets in the Middle East reported attempted strikes in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan, and Iraq. Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry also said Iran targeted a Saudi tanker in the Strait of Hormuz and killed members of its crew.
As of 4 p.m. Eastern time and 11 p.m. in much of the Middle East, CENTCOM had not announced additional strikes. Trump told reporters that the U.S. is “prepared to do another one anytime we want.”
CENTCOM continues to enforce a blockade of Iranian ships and ports and said in a Sept. 2 social media post that it has redirected 86 commercial vessels, disabled three, and boarded two as part of the blockade.

articles.title: Twenty Ukrainian firms are racing to catch Russia’s jet-powered Shaheds. This one’s interceptor is already flying combat missions
articles.body:
Twenty Ukrainian companies are now building jet-powered interceptors to down Russia's increasingly fast jet-powered drones. One of them, the Ukrainian-British startup Firebolt Engineering, already has an interceptor flying combat missions with two Air Force units and Ukraine's special operations forces, Defender Media reports.
Russia launched more than 2,500 jet-powered drones at Ukraine in August alone, straining air defenses built to catch the slower, piston-engine Shahed-136. Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said on 30 August 2026 that four interceptor systems have cleared field testing and are being scaled toward mass production. It is unclear whether Griffen, Firebolt's drone, is among them.
Grenadyr funds a spinout
Firebolt was spun out after the UK-based investment fund Grenadyr backed the team behind the interceptor project. Grenadyr's director, Tomasz Wozniak, told the outlet that a reliable way to intercept jet-powered Shaheds "has never been more important" as Russia scales up the faster drones.
Grenadyr and Firebolt have not disclosed the size of the investment, though the fund's check ranged from $350,000 to $1.3 million.
The new company employs up to 25 people across Ukraine and the UK, split into component manufacturing, final assembly, and calibration, plus a separate R&D unit. Its CEO, who asked to be identified only as Mykola, led the interceptor project prior to the spinout.
Griffen flies, but not against jets yet
Griffen, Firebolt's first product, is a fixed-wing, jet-powered interceptor that reaches speeds above 350 km/h, altitudes above 7.5 km, and a range of up to 120 km, according to Defender Media. Mykola said the team aims to push its speed past 400 km/h through aerodynamic changes. The drone currently costs an estimated $8,300–$10,500.
Griffen still flies on Chinese engines while its British partner, Dynamic Propulsion, develops a turbojet built specifically for the drone, with test samples expected by the end of summer. Firebolt can build 30 Griffens a month and is working to add more crews to fly them, Mykola said. The drone's first confirmed kill, however, was a conventional-engine Geran — not the jet-powered variant it was designed to catch.
Autonomy waits on Ukraine's radars
Firebolt is developing a homing system meant to let Griffen find and strike targets without an operator, a goal shared by rival interceptor makers The Fourth Law, SkyFall, and F-Drones. The system is in testing and expected to ship by default by mid-fall, Mykola said.
Full autonomy, he added, is bottlenecked by Ukraine's radar coverage, which he described as too thin and fragmented to reliably feed target data to an autonomous drone. Closing that gap, he said, depends on the state buying more radars — a decision outside Firebolt's control.

articles.title: Taiwan reveals NT$36 billion budget for Strong Bow missile system
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Air Force will spend NT$36.04 billion (US$1.13 billion) through 2032 to develop and procure the indigenous Strong Bow medium-altitude anti-tactical ballistic missile system.
The system is designed to intercept tactical ballistic missiles with ranges of up to 1,000 kilometers and will complement the nation’s existing lower-tier missile defense systems, per Liberty Times. The ministry said the system is being developed as part of a multilayered defense strategy to counter the growing ballistic missile threat from China.
Strong Bow was originally expected to be funded through a proposed NT$1.25 trillion special defense budget, but was not included in the final proposal. The 2027 budget documents submitted to the Legislative Yuan instead show that the program will be funded through the defense ministry’s annual budget.
The Cabinet said Strong Bow was originally among 23 weapons programs planned under the proposed special defense budget, but was shifted to the annual budget after the legislature approved NT$780 billion for US arms purchases, per CNA. The government said the defense ministry has since prioritized programs based on delivery schedules and operational needs, although the broader military buildup timeline has been affected.
The ministry did not disclose the number of missiles or weapons systems to be procured, citing classified information, Liberty Times reported. It said the missiles and associated weapons systems are scheduled for delivery starting in 2028.
The Strong Bow system is designed for mobile deployment to improve survivability and can operate alongside other air defense missile systems under a unified command-and-control structure. Its two-stage missile consists of an interceptor vehicle and booster, uses a composite-material casing, and employs thrust-vector control during the terminal phase to adjust its trajectory and improve interception capabilities at medium and high altitudes.
The missile uses a millimeter-wave radar seeker to detect and track targets, while its fire-control radar is the first domestically developed active electronically scanned array radar, according to Liberty Times. Military sources said the radar has a longer detection range than that of the radars on existing Patriot and Sky Bow III systems.

articles.title: Israeli strikes kill one in south Lebanon as Rome talks stall
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israeli strikes kill one in south Lebanon as Rome talks remain stalled
Israeli strikes killed one person and wounded another in the southern Lebanese city of Nabatieh on Wednesday, according to Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency, after the Israeli military said it had struck the area in response to an alleged Hezbollah drone attack on its forces.
The NNA said the casualties resulted from an Israeli drone strike on the al-Ruwaiss and al-Maasouma Garden neighbourhoods of Nabatieh. Further Israeli strikes later hit the Nabatieh area, with local media reporting heavy explosions around Kfar Tebnit and circulating footage of a large column of smoke.
The Israeli military claimed that Hezbollah had launched two explosive drones overnight towards soldiers operating near the Ali al-Taher Ridge, close to Nabatieh. It said troops fired at and intercepted one of the drones and that no Israeli personnel were injured. Israel said it subsequently targeted what it alleged to be "Hezbollah infrastructure" used to plan attacks on its troops and civilians.
Hezbollah had not publicly commented on the Israeli allegation by Wednesday afternoon. The group has not claimed responsibility for attacks on Israeli targets in recent weeks.
Air raid sirens sounded briefly on Tuesday night in Tuval and Ma’ayan Baruch in northern Israel, near the Lebanese border, amid the alleged drone incident. Lebanese media later reported additional Israeli attacks across the south, including in Mansouri, Houla and Qantara.
The Ali al-Taher Ridge, a high point near Nabatieh overlooking areas of south Lebanon and northern Israel, has become a particular focus of Israeli operations. Israel has alleged that Hezbollah maintains underground military infrastructure in the area, while the elevation gives forces operating there a wide view of the surrounding border region.
Rome talks remain deadlocked
The attacks came a day after US Ambassador to Lebanon Michel Issa and US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem. Israeli National Security Adviser Shmuel Ben Ezra also attended the meeting, according to images issued by Netanyahu’s office, which did not disclose the substance of the discussion.
The meeting took place before an anticipated eighth round of US-mediated Lebanese-Israeli talks in Rome. No official date has been announced, though Lebanese broadcaster MTV reported that the next session could be held on 15-16 September. In a statement on X, Huckabee claimed Hezbollah was the only obstacle to progress in the negotiations.
The talks are based on a US-brokered framework agreed on 26 June, under which Israeli forces would withdraw in phases from southern Lebanon while the Lebanese army deploys to designated areas and non-state armed infrastructure is dismantled. The arrangement has been slowed by disagreements over the sequencing of any Israeli withdrawal, the scope and pace of the Lebanese army’s deployment, and how compliance would be independently verified.
Israel has demanded assurances that areas transferred to Lebanese state control are clear of Hezbollah weapons and military positions. Lebanon, meanwhile, has sought a further Israeli withdrawal and resisted proposals that could amount to a permanent "security belt" or buffer zone inside its territory. Hezbollah has rejected arrangements affecting its weapons, leaving the army’s role in any eventual implementation politically sensitive.
Separately, the Lebanese Armed Forces said it was responding to what it described as "fabricated claims" by Israeli media concerning the army’s positions and operational role in southern Lebanon. In a statement issued on Wednesday, it said the reports sought to undermine internal cohesion and public confidence in the institution and its leadership.
The statement did not identify a specific report or outlets. But it appears to be intended to counter claims often by Israeli media outlets to cast doubt on the Lebanon army’s performance, loyalties or ability to carry out its southern missions at a moment when it is expected to be central to any eventual Israeli withdrawal and security arrangement. The army said its personnel remained committed to the command’s directives and to defending Lebanese sovereignty, security and stability.
Lebanon's health ministry says Israeli attacks have killed at least 8,920 people since hostilities erupted in October 2023.

articles.title: Persian Gulf equilibrium: The fracturing of US hegemony
articles.body:
Persian Gulf equilibrium: The fracturing of US hegemony
TEHRAN — The metaphor of Tom and Jerry has long served financial journalists describing the Federal Reserve's pressure on Wall Street. That narrative, however, is a sideshow. The real contest unfolds in the Persian Gulf, and the dynamics defy cartoon logic entirely. Iran, cast as Jerry, does not flee; it stands its ground, exhausts its adversary, and systematically neutralizes American capabilities.
The International Monetary Fund's 2026 Persian Gulf economic projections offer a stark revelation. Iran's economy is forecast to contract by 6.1 percent this year, a severe blow attributable to American sanctions. Yet Qatar, home to the Al Udeid Air Base and a cornerstone of US regional strategy, is projected to shrink by 8.6 percent, with Kuwait also registering negative growth. The nation Washington seeks to isolate is outperforming its closest allies, rendering the administration's declared "most crushing economic operation" a self-defeating exercise that has inflicted greater harm on friends than on the designated foe.
This outcome stems from two strategic factors. Iranian strikes crippled Qatar's Ras Laffan liquefied natural gas complex—the world's largest removing approximately 17 percent of its export capacity with repairs requiring three to five years. More consequentially, Iran's effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz has severed Qatar's primary revenue route to European markets. Doha responded with a 30 percent reduction in departmental budgets and an 85 percent cut to overseas aid. The emirate's vulnerability exposes a fundamental failure of its American patron to guarantee maritime security, undermining Washington's protective commitments.
Militarily, the United States confronts a depletion of its advanced interceptor inventory. Patriot and THAAD systems have been drawn down to critically low levels, with some estimates indicating losses of up to three-fifths of total stockpiles. Requests from Saudi Arabia for replenishment have been denied, revealing an arsenal stretched beyond capacity. Iran has exploited this asymmetry through a cost-exchange strategy: deploying inexpensive, mass-produced drones that compel the US to expend million-dollar interceptors per engagement. This arithmetic has exhausted American defensive resources, forcing a strategic reevaluation.
The conflict's impetus traces directly to Israeli advocacy for direct US military confrontation with Iran. Washington's compliance has, however, transformed American military installations across the Persian Gulf from protective shields into liability magnets. Persian Gulf Arab monarchies have consequently initiated back-channel communications with Tehran, as confirmed by Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf. Their calculus reflects a sober assessment that the US security umbrella no longer functions, with Patriot batteries depleted and alliance commitments hollowed out.
For these states, a homegrown regional order now appears as the sole viable alternative. Iran has demonstrated resilience through sustained sanctions, bombing campaigns, and strategic retention of its nuclear and missile programs while exercising precise control over the Strait of Hormuz. This endurance has compelled Washington to negotiate on Iranian terms. Unlike the Federal Reserve's domestic measures raising interest rates to suppress demand Iran offers cooperation and trade routes rather than occupation and regime change.
The empirical evidence is unequivocal. IMF projections confirm the economic paradox. Depleted American arsenals validate the military imbalance. Diplomatic overtures from Riyadh and Abu Dhabi signal the collapse of US strategic credibility. Iran has not merely survived the most powerful empire; it has emerged as the indispensable regional power. The Zionist project for regional hegemony lies buried beneath Qatar's damaged LNG infrastructure and the empty Patriot canisters across Saudi bases. The American cat retreats, its claws broken, while Iran assumes its position at the center of a new Persian Gulf order, one that Arab monarchies in the Persian Gulf, after decades of servitude, are finally embracing.
The old balance is giving way to something more uncertain. Iran has not emerged stronger because it escaped the costs of war, but because, despite those costs, it remains impossible to exclude from any serious settlement of the Gulf's future. The real question is no longer whether Iran can be pushed to the margins, but whether Washington can still dictate regional rules as it once did. In the Persian Gulf, Jerry has stopped running. He has found his ground, raised his voice, and forced the cat to reckon with him. Tom may still be larger, richer, and more heavily armed but size alone no longer guarantees control. The next chapter will be written by those capable of enduring pressure and shaping what comes after it.

articles.title: World News in Brief: US-Iran war intensifies, aid for Myanmar, casualties in Ukraine
articles.body:
World News in Brief: US-Iran war intensifies, aid for Myanmar, casualties in Ukraine
Fighting between the United States and Iran has sharply escalated after a month-long lull, with the two sides exchanging strikes as fears grow over further civilian casualties.
The US military struck rocket launchers on an island in the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, days after US President Donald Trump announced that American forces had cleared all mines from the crucial trade route.
The US said the weekend strikes were aimed at preventing Iran from laying new mines.
After Iranian missiles launched towards Jordan in retaliation were intercepted, the US struck targets it claims were linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
According to Iranian authorities, US strikes hit a wedding party in Kuhestak on Wednesday, killing at least four and injuring 68 more.
The US military said it is investigating the incident and that it never targets civilians.
The latest exchange marks a major escalation in the conflict that began in February, when the US and Israel launched military operations against Iran.
Condemnation from Guterres
UN Secretary-General António Guterres expressed grave concern over the escalation and reported rise in civilian casualties, including at the wedding party.
“The Secretary-General condemns all attacks against civilians,” UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said.
“He recalls that all parties must respect their obligations under international humanitarian law, including the principles of distinction, proportionality and precautions.”
Mr. Guterres strongly encouraged the US and Iran to return to diplomacy to avoid the “devastating consequences” further escalation would have on civilians across the Middle East.
UN launches aid transport service in Myanmar
The UN’s World Food Programme (WFP) has launched an emergency cargo transport service to help humanitarian partners in Myanmar deliver lifesaving assistance to flood-stricken areas.
The logistics service – free for UN partners to use – is initially focusing on the towns of Lemyethna, Yegyi and Ngathaingchaung, which have been hit hard by floods in the past few months that have displaced thousands of families.
“When floodwaters isolate entire communities, logistics becomes the difference between success and failure of an operation,” WFP Myanmar Country Director Michael Dunford said.
“Beyond delivering our own food assistance, WFP is serving as the logistics provider for the wider humanitarian response.”
Collective effort
For at least two weeks, WFP will transport food and nutrition assistance; water, sanitation and hygiene supplies; medicines; and emergency shelter materials to civilians in hard-to-reach areas.
“By opening our transport lines to our partners, we can collectively ensure that food, medicine, and shelter materials swiftly and safely reach those who need them most,” Mr. Dunford said.
WFP has also launched an emergency food response in Myanmar’s Sagaing Region, which was hit especially hard by an earthquake earlier this year and already faces conflict, widespread restrictions to access and connectivity challenges.
The agency has already reached 15,000 people with emergency rations in the Ayeyarwady and Sagaing regions.
Russian attacks kill more civilians in Ukraine
Russian attacks on Ukraine between Tuesday and Wednesday morning killed at least 12 civilians and injured more than 65 others, causing casualties across six regions, according to the UN’s humanitarian aid office (OCHA).
The attacks damaged homes, schools, a shopping centre and a postal hub. Strikes on energy facilities caused power outages in several regions.
Power generation equipment at a utility plant in Kherson was destroyed, raising fears that families unable to move to safer regions could lack heat and electricity in the coming winter.
“This escalation inflicts a devastating and growing toll on civilians by destroying livelihoods, worsening the psychological burden and disrupting daily life,” said Matthias Schmale, the UN’s humanitarian coordinator in Ukraine. “We must never normalise this.”
Meanwhile, German officials have accused Russia of authorising an attempted explosive drone attack at Leipzig Airport on 4 August. Russian officials have denied any involvement.
Humanitarian facilities destroyed
A humanitarian warehouse contracted by the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) was destroyed in a Russian attack on 27 August in Chubynske, Kyiv region, destroying lifesaving supplies intended for children and families.
“This impedes the delivery of vital support to the most vulnerable, especially as another harsh winter approaches,” UNICEF said.
In recent days, a missile strike also destroyed the humanitarian warehouses and vehicles of a UN-partnered NGO in Sumy, and another strike damaged an NGO-operated evacuation bus in Donetsk.
These attacks are part of a wider pattern of Russian strikes. At least six warehouses belonging to humanitarian organizations – including UN agencies, the Ukrainian Red Cross Society and NGOs – were impacted by Russian attacks in August.
“Our partners continue to provide medical and psychological aid, hot meals and shelter materials to support the humanitarian response,” Mr. Dujarric said.

articles.title: Trump touts Hormuz control, credits US strikes for halting Iran’s nuclear programme
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said that Iran must never be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon, crediting last year's US strikes with halting Tehran's atomic programme just before completion and adding, "We now control the Strait of Hormuz."
Speaking in a phone interview published on Wednesday, Trump said: "If we didn't do it, Iran would have a nuclear weapon."
"If we didn't send in the B-2 bombers a year ago to blow up their nuclear capacity, you know they were two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon," he said.
Warning of consequences, Trump argued that if Iran had "a nuclear weapon, Israel would be gone. The Middle East would be gone, and they would be hitting cities in the United States, absolutely, because they're crazy."
Turning to the latest strikes, Trump said, "We're doing very well. We're just annihilating them, but the bottom line on that is very simple: Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon."
‘Control of Hormuz’
He said US forces now dominate a key regional waterway, adding, "We now control the Strait of Hormuz. We control it. Last night, we took out 28 boats, 28 ships. We control it. They get nothing, and we took out ships."
Trump also suggested in a social media post renaming the Strait of Hormuz as "Trump Strait".
"Now that we have it under USA control, should we change the name of the Hormuz Strait to the Trump Strait??? Like America itself, it would be 'hotter' than ever before!" Trump said on his Truth Social network.
Regional tensions have escalated following US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began on Feb. 28 and Tehran's retaliatory missile and drone attacks against Israel and US interests in countries across the region.
Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding on June 18 concerning freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, but its implementation has stalled amid disagreements over security arrangements in the strait.

articles.title: China's Xi holds talks with Egypt's Sisi
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
China's Xi holds talks with Sisi in first Egypt visit in a decade
Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Wednesday received his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping on his first visit to Cairo in a decade, as Beijing seeks a greater foothold in the region against the backdrop of the US-Iran war.
The 21-gun salute at Cairo's Ittihadiya Palace marked the start of a day of talks expected to cover the Middle East war and its fallout, including on maritime trade security, as well as boosting Chinese investment in the Arab world's most populous country.
The two BRICS members are expected to sign a slate of economic agreements, including on artificial intelligence, transport and manufacturing.
Egypt currently estimates Chinese investments at around $10 billion. Beijing has key stakes in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, which are only expected to grow as the US-Iran war threatens global maritime trade.
Beijing has also played a key role in Sisi's megaprojects, the crowning jewel of which is the New Administrative Capital 50 kilometres (30 miles) east of Cairo, large swathes of which have been bankrolled by Chinese investment.
China is a major exporter to Egypt, with its trade surplus reaching $12 billion in the first seven months of 2026, according to Chinese customs data.
Across Cairo, a megalopolis home to over 26 million people, major streets have been lined with Chinese and Egyptian flags, as well as billboards showing Sisi and Xi.
Street signs boast of "generations of Egyptian-Chinese friendship flowing like the Nile River", while residents have been warned to plan for substantial traffic delays on their commutes.
Xi is expected to traverse the entire capital during his visit Wednesday, including a stop at the Grand Egyptian Museum overlooking the Giza Pyramids.
'Independent foreign policy'
According to analysts, Cairo will use the summit to underscore its strategic autonomy, showing it can leverage its close ties with both Washington and Beijing.
Sisi, in an op-ed published in Egyptian media on Tuesday, highlighted Cairo's "independent foreign policy", days after a branch of Egypt's second-largest bank was targeted by US sanctions.
He wrote that Egypt and China were partners in "strengthening the role of the global south" in an increasingly polarised world.
Washington vowed last month to isolate Iran economically, threatening expanded sanctions that could also hit Chinese banks, among others.
China, a major buyer of Iranian oil, has vowed to safeguard its interests.
In the lead-up to an expected meeting between Xi and US President Donald Trump this month, it has also sought to shore up ties with US-friendly regional nations.
Egypt is one of the largest recipients of US military aid, and historically a key Middle East mediator.
Last week, the US Treasury announced sanctions on the Emirati branch of Egypt's Banque Misr for alleged support to Iran.
Egypt—which under Sisi's administration became one of the world's top weapons buyers—hosted major joint air combat exercises with the Chinese military in August, featuring Beijing's powerful J-16 fighter jet.

articles.title: Leaked Documents Reveal Covert Russian Missile Technology Transfer to Iran
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Leaked Documents Reveal Covert Russian Missile Technology Transfer to Iran
Russia has been secretly helping Iran develop advanced supersonic cruise missiles through a multiyear covert technology transfer program, according to an investigation by the Financial Times, posted on September 1.
Codenamed “C430L,” the program began in 2023 and has continued into 2026.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
This advanced technology transfer is part of a broader military exchange between the two nations. It was previously reported that Russia is simultaneously using the landlocked Caspian Sea to ship explosives, ammunition, and drone components directly to Tehran, bypassing Western navies to help replenish Iranian military stocks following strikes by the US and Israel.
According to leaked Russian correspondence, travel records, and military patents obtained by the Financial Times, the initiative focuses on helping Tehran develop a ramjet propulsion system—a specialized engine that enables cruise missiles to sustain flight at several times the speed of sound.
Missile experts told the publication the technology is designed for anti-ship and land-attack cruise missiles capable of threatening naval vessels and missile defense systems in the Middle East.
The program was arranged by Russia’s state arms exporter, Rosoboronexport, in coordination with defense contractor NPO Mashinostroyenia. Financial Times noted that senior Russian missile designers and propulsion specialists made repeated trips to Iran to assist with the project.
According to the Financial Times, NPO Mashinostroyenia engineers received technical data from an Iranian flight test and provided detailed technical analysis to help troubleshoot combustion, fuel system, and airflow issues in the Iranian prototype.
While Iran has previously flight-tested ramjet components, mastering supersonic air-breathing propulsion has remained a key technological hurdle for its defense industry.
The Financial Times reported that correspondence between Russian and Iranian officials regarding the next development phase of C430L continued through mid-2026.
Russia’s export revenues have also temporarily surged by 27% year-over-year in the second quarter to $125.7 billion, driven by global energy price spikes and Middle East supply disruptions. Driven by climbing Urals crude prices and expanded agricultural quotas, the brief foreign currency influx strengthened the ruble through late May.
