articles.title: What a new Black Sea grain crisis means for the Middle East
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
What a new Black Sea grain crisis means for the Middle East
Ukrainian drones struck Russian cargo ships carrying stolen Ukrainian grain in the Sea of Azov in April.
Since then, drone attacks by both sides have intensified in the Black Sea region, continuing throughout the summer months.
"For Ukraine, targeting Russia’s oil revenues - and particularly the so-called shadow fleet that enables Moscow to circumvent sanctions - is an important part of increasing the economic cost of the war and degrading Russia’s ability to finance and sustain its military operations," Dr Yevgeniya Gaber, a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Turkey Program, told The New Arab.
In August, two Turkish-owned civilian ships, the Yaşar and the Nadezhda, were struck by drones after departing from the Russian port of Novorossiysk. In response, Turkey’s Foreign Ministry called for the safe passage of commercial shipping through the Black Sea.
“Russia has fewer sea drones, but it is using both planes and drones to track the Ukrainian navy. For Russia, the Black Sea is now mainly used to strike southern Ukraine and protect their own commercial shipping, since their fleet is now hidden in ports,” Clément Molin, an open-source analyst following the Ukraine conflict, told The New Arab.
“Ukraine’s UAVs are being constantly used to track Russian ships, and more than 200 commercial ships have been targeted, mainly from [Russia’s] ghost fleet,” he said. “Ukraine has barely any navy but managed to create a new dimension of the war at sea with drones.”
No ceasefire in sight
On 13 August, Ukrainian drones hit the Russian port facility of Novorossiysk, damaging two grain export terminals. It wasn’t long before Russia carried out a wave of strikes in Ukraine’s Odesa Oblast, hitting food storage infrastructure.
“Russian forces have targeted Ukrainian ports, grain terminals, silos and export infrastructure throughout the war. What has changed is the scale and intensity of the pressure, including more attacks on civilian commercial vessels, warehouses and food-related infrastructure,” Gaber said.
“The consequences are particularly serious for agricultural exports and, therefore, for food security well beyond Ukraine. Between 1 and 26 August, Ukraine exported only 822,000 tonnes of grain - around 21 percent of what it could normally have exported with functioning logistics," she added.
"Total agricultural exports, including grain, oilseeds, oils and meals, amounted to approximately 1.4 million tonnes, only around one-third of Ukraine’s potential export capacity during this period, according to the Ukrainian government."
On 27 August, The Wall Street Journal reported that wheat prices had reached a three-year high as the Black Sea fighting disrupted grain exports, with Odesa and Novorossiysk losing export capacity.
In late August, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Russia was not ready for a ceasefire on grain shipments in the Black Sea. Moscow reportedly sought to include an end to attacks on Russian energy infrastructure in the agreement.
The Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure have been a key way for Kyiv to bring the war back home to Russia after four and a half years of the full-scale invasion.
“The problem is not limited to attacks on ships themselves. Russia is targeting the infrastructure that makes maritime trade possible: ports, grain silos, warehouses, railway connections and other logistical nodes,” Gaber told The New Arab.
“In July alone, Russia carried out 67 attacks on Ukrainian seaport infrastructure, 35 attacks on civilian vessels in ports, and 22 attacks on vessels operating through the Ukrainian maritime corridor.”
The attacks come as both Russia and Ukraine are in peak harvest season, and the grain will go to waste unless it is exported soon. Major commercial shipping firms are suspending operations due to the threat of drones in the Black Sea.
“This creates longer-term economic damage as well. Ukrainian farmers lose revenue from exports and face higher logistical costs, reducing the capital available to invest in the next planting season,” Gaber said.
Diplomatic tensions
The Turkish Foreign Ministry warned that the attacks could have “multifaceted negative repercussions”, including for food security.
“We therefore reiterate our call to all relevant actors, particularly the warring parties, to urgently implement concrete measures to ensure the safety of navigation in the Black Sea.”
The collapse of the Black Sea Grain Initiative, which Turkey had helped facilitate, effectively ended in the summer of 2023. However, Ukraine and Russia were still able to ship their agricultural products to the international market by staying close to the coastlines.
To mitigate any diplomatic blowback, Scott Lucas, Professor of International Politics at University College Dublin’s Clinton Institute, told The New Arab that Ukraine could signal that “we don’t want to be in this situation…of having to counter-attack against the Russian vessels in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. The Russians put us in this situation”.
The politics surrounding grain shipments from the Black Sea to the Middle East have become an increasingly sensitive issue. The Ukrainian Foreign Ministry noted that stolen grain exported by Russia was reaching Turkey, Egypt, and Algeria.
In April, Ukraine and Israel exchanged accusations over a Russian shadow fleet vessel that arrived in Israel carrying grain from the occupied Ukrainian territories.
“Diplomatically, Ukraine has limited means to stop these attacks as long as Russia is unwilling to respond to calls for de-escalation. Kyiv has repeatedly called for a ceasefire and negotiations to end the war, while Moscow has continued to intensify attacks on critical infrastructure," Gaber said.
"This is why Ukraine argues that diplomacy has to be backed by greater economic, political and military pressure on Russia. Middle Eastern countries also have an interest in making this message clear.”
Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports and commercial shipping are not simply a bilateral Russian-Ukrainian issue, she said, as they directly affect the reliability and cost of food imports and therefore regional food security.
Syria and Egypt's food security
Over 90 percent of Ukraine’s agricultural exports are shipped through seaports, with countries in the Middle East especially vulnerable to prolonged disruptions in the global food supplies. Many have taken steps to mitigate these risks. In the spring, for example, Egypt reached a deal to receive grain shipments from Russia.
“In the case of Egypt, [it depends on] how much backstop they have from the Gulf States. Do they have alternative sources for supply?” Lucas told The New Arab.
Roughly 80 percent of Egypt’s wheat imports came from Black Sea ports in the first half of 2026.
The Emirati company Al Dahra Agriculture Trading and Egypt’s General Authority for Supply Commodities recently signed a five-year, $500 million wheat supply agreement. Egypt’s government has also imposed price controls on unsubsidised bread since March. In mid-August, Egypt expanded a cash subsidy scheme to cover more food items.
“Anytime you get a disruption to grain supplies, especially in countries that are already in a tenuous economic situation, you have to run it on a case-by-case basis on how well these countries prepared for such a shock. 2010 is a reminder of what can happen quickly,” Lucas added.
A poor harvest and high food prices in 2010 contributed to the uprising against the former regime of Bashar Al-Assad in Syria, which lasted nearly 14 years.
“A lot of countries don’t want Syria to fail,” Lucas said, explaining that Syria could likely rely on Turkish and US assistance since the Trump Administration is interested in maintaining Syrian stability.
Likewise, Ukraine has sought to build up its own avenues of cooperation with the new Syrian government.
“During President Zelensky’s visit to Damascus in April, food security was one of the issues discussed with President Ahmed al-Sharaa, alongside broader security and trade cooperation. Ukraine has offered to support Syria through initiatives such as Grain from Ukraine,” Gaber told The New Arab.
Syria has made progress in increasing its own domestic production of wheat. Benjamin Fève, a Senior Consultant at Karam Shaar Advisory Limited, told The New Arab that for now, Syria’s food supply was relatively safe.
“Syria had a very successful harvest. Its strategic reserves have been replenished, and Syria will be much less dependent on imports. Even if the food supplies are secure in the short term, in the medium and long term, they are not, given the huge variability in harvests and wheat production overall,” he said.
“In order to make Arabic flat bread, a staple food in Syria, you need 80 percent of soft wheat and 20 percent of hard wheat,” Fève added.
“Syria exports its surplus of hard wheat at a premium and imports less expensive soft wheat. Depending on where Syria sources its soft wheat, disruptions could cause food insecurity.”
Restarting negotiations
Changing weather patterns, conflicts, and high fuel prices are still significant concerns and could affect the food security of tens of millions of people dependent on the international grain trade. Still, the possibility of talks or a new Black Sea Grain Initiative between Russia and Ukraine appears distant.
“While Ukraine is offering additional grain supplies to countries that need them, Russia is attacking the ports, storage facilities and logistical infrastructure required to produce, store and export that grain,” Gaber told The New Arab.
The risk for the countries in the Mediterranean region and beyond remains present as long as the conflict shuts down the grain transits through the Black Sea.
“For Ukraine to play a stabilising role in food security across the Middle East and Africa, it first needs to be able to maintain production and secure access to the Black Sea. At present, Russia remains the principal obstacle to both," Gaber added.
Lucas noted that Ukraine has to find a way to get Russia to the negotiating table. “That hand was played very well by the Turks in supporting Ukraine in 2022. Can you do the same thing here?”
But while Ukraine has indicated that it wants to negotiate, Russia continues to pursue maximum demands.
The United States and the international community would have to put more pressure on Russia to reach an agreement. “If you can get that type of political strategy, you can put the onus on the Russians,” Lucas said.
Christopher Solomon is a Middle East analyst, researcher, editor, and writer based in the Washington, DC area. He is the author of the book In Search of Greater Syria (Bloomsbury)
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Nuclear bomb test veterans were victims of one of ‘greatest scandals in Britain’, says ex-defence minister
articles.body:
A former defence minister has admitted misleading parliament over the existence of crucial medical records relating to nuclear bomb test veterans.
Tobias Ellwood has said he unwittingly gave MPs incorrect information in 2018 when he told them he had been unable to locate information on veterans’ blood tests after being given incorrect information by officials at the Ministry of Defence (MoD).
Veterans have been fighting for years to see the records as many look to prove that years of serious illnesses such as cancer were linked to their experiences testing nuclear weapons. Ellwood’s admission will increase pressure on the MoD to explain whether its officials have helped prevent those veterans get justice.
In a piece for the Guardian, Ellwood says: “In December 2018, as defence minister, I inadvertently misled parliament.
“Asked whether blood samples had been taken from service personnel for radiological monitoring during the nuclear bomb tests, I relayed the line provided to me by the Ministry of Defence: it was ‘unable to locate any information’ suggesting blood samples had been taken for radiological monitoring at the tests.
“I now know the reality was very different – these samples were taken across the armed services branches. But those veterans seeking compensation for serious illnesses developed after radiation exposure have been unable to access them.”
He added: “This is among the greatest scandals in Britain, and it must be addressed.”
An MoD spokesperson said: “This government commissioned and completed an extensive records discovery exercise, examining tens of thousands of documents to address long-standing questions from veterans about blood and urine testing policies during the nuclear testing programme.
“The findings have now been published in full, following regular engagement between ministers, nuclear test veterans and community groups throughout the process.”
Between 1952 and 1967, about 22,000 British military personnel took part in 45 large-scale nuclear weapons tests in Australia and the South Pacific. Some pilots flew through mushroom clouds, some troops crawled through fallout and many witnessed the first test wearing little more than short-sleeved shirts and shorts.
Large numbers later suffered blood disorders and cancers, which they believed were caused by exposure to radioactive fallout. Most were denied pensions because of their ill health.
Unlike other nuclear-armed countries such as France, the US and the Soviet Union, the UK has never compensated those involved in testing atomic bombs.
The case has been compared with the infected blood scandal, which saw more than 30,000 people contract HIV and Hepatitis C in the the 1970s and early 1990s after being given contaminated blood and blood products.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has previously said he was misled by officials when he claimed as health secretary in 2009 that there was no evidence that people were knowingly given contaminated blood. His claims echo those being made today by Ellwood.
Burnham has also been a vocal supporter of the nuclear test veterans in recent years.
As Greater Manchester mayor in 2022, Burnham said: “If the state was conducting medical tests upon servicemen and not informing them when they found serious irregularity, that is at least misconduct in public office, and more serious, perhaps gross negligence manslaughter, in respect of people who died as a result.
“Crimes have been committed.”
The prime minister is now coming under pressure to begin an inquiry and allocate government money for compensation to the victims.
One of the major problems with securing compensation so far has been the lack of medical evidence linking veterans’ health problems to their experiences helping with nuclear tests.
The government long maintained that it did not hold any such medical records – a claim that was proved incorrect in 2022 when the journalist Susie Boniface revealed the existence of a database of 28,000 documents known as Merlin.
That database had been put together in response to a 2007 lawsuit by 1,000 British test veterans and their families, but the information was classified.
Ellwood says he did not find out about the existence of this database until 2022, when details began to emerge in the press.
He writes in his piece: “If this information existed within the MoD, why had ministers not been given the full picture?”

articles.title: Videos and debris raise questions over alleged US strike on Iranian wedding
articles.body:
Videos and debris raise questions over alleged US strike on Iranian wedding
On the evening of September 1, a barrage of US missile and drone attacks on a town in southern Iran allegedly struck a wedding ceremony, killing at least five people, including a four-year-old boy. FRANCE 24 geolocated a direct hit to the civilian building where local residents say the wedding was being held. The building was more than 135 meters from the apparent target, a communications tower.
Amateur videos showing the aftermath of a US attack on September 1 on the building show extensive destruction. The roof of the building, located in Kuhestak, Hormozgan province, along Iran’s southern Persian Gulf coast, appears to have been completely destroyed, with debris scattered for dozens of metres around the impact site. Videos from a hospital in Minab, 45 km to the north, also show people injured in the attack, including children being treated, as well as the body of a boy, covered with a blue sheet.
According to the Iranian Red Crescent, five people were killed and 68 others were injured in the attack.
To display this content from Telegram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
"There’s absolutely no military infrastructure near that house"
"Motahereh7", a resident of the town with a large following on Instagram, posted a video shortly after the airstrikes at around 9:30pm local time saying she had been attending a wedding at the site.
"Lots of you sent me messages asking, 'Have they hit Kuhestak?'. Yes, they hit the house where there was a wedding. It’s my husband’s cousin’s house. I don’t know yet how many people were there, how many people are under [the rubble]… God help us. There’s absolutely no military infrastructure near that house. Nothing…"
To display this content from Instagram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
What do we know about the attack?
A CCTV video that captured the impact on the town shows at least six explosions. The apparent primary target was a communications tower on the edge of the town, on the shore of the Persian Gulf. Videos recorded by local residents also documented strikes on the tower.
To display this content from Telegram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
FRANCE 24 geolocated the communications tower and found it to be located in an urban area, just 30 metres from the nearest buildings.
To display this content from Telegram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
To display this content from Instagram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Several videos showing the aftermath indicate that the building where the wedding was said to be taking place was directly hit, rather than damaged by shrapnel. Using several videos recorded by local residents, FRANCE 24 geolocated the building and found that it was more than 135 metres from the communications tower.
To display this content from Telegram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
According to several experts, remnants of missile debris recovered from the impact site suggest that a SLAM-ER cruise missile may have been used. Boeing, the missile’s manufacturer, describes the SLAM-ER as the most accurate weapon in the US Navy’s inventory.
However, FRANCE 24 could not independently confirm whether the debris was recovered from the site of the strike on the wedding, or from the communications tower.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Several Iranian officials reacted to the incident. Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker and a key figure in negotiations with the United States, called the US government "Satan".
Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for US Central Command, said they were aware of reports of civilian casualties. He added: "The US military never targets civilians, unlike the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)."
This is the fourth reported incident in which US strikes have hit civilian sites in Iran since the US-Israel war against Iran began in February 2026.
On February 28, the first day of the war, a strike reportedly carried out by the United States killed about 170 people, most of them schoolchildren, as well as teachers, parents and others.

articles.title: Xi calls on Mideast nations to be ‘masters of their own affairs’ in rare Egypt visit
articles.body:
Xi calls on Mideast nations to be ‘masters of their own affairs’ in rare Egypt visit
Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday called on "the people of the Middle East" to oppose "externalinterference" and consider reshaping the region's security order during a visit to Egypt. The rare visit by the Chinese leader comes as Beijing aims to expand its influence in the region as the Iran war tests the reliability of the traditional US security umbrella in a vital geostrategic zone.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday urged countries to oppose "external interference" in the Middle East and said Beijing was ready to work with regional states to safeguard maritime shipping, jeopardised by the US-Iran war.
Xi's remarks to his Egyptian counterpart Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, on his first visit to Cairo in a decade, come as Beijing seeks a greater foothold in the region, expanding investment while managing fallout from the war.
"We must uphold the principle that the people of the Middle East are the masters of their own affairs, oppose external interference [and] support regional countries in strengthening dialogue on peace and security," Xi said in a meeting with Sisi, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua.
Xi was greeted by Sisi and a 21-gun salute for talks at the opulent Ittihadiya Presidential Palace in the Egyptian capital.
The talks covered the six-month US-Iran conflict, with both presidents urging "diplomatic solutions" to reach a "comprehensive agreement to end the war", according to a statement from Sisi's spokesperson.
Sisi's office also said the two BRICS members signed an agreement to launch the third phase of the Egyptian-Chinese industrial zone at the Suez Canal, which officials say already hosts 200 companies and investments worth around $4 billion.
The new investments – for which Egypt has not announced a figure – give Beijing even greater influence in the canal zone, a critical artery of global trade, as conflict in the region chokes other conduits.
Read moreGlobal shipping firms to avoid Suez Canal as attacks from Yemen's Houthi rebels increase
Xi said China "stands ready to work with countries in the region to safeguard the security of international shipping lanes, advance development cooperation... and eliminate the breeding grounds for conflict".
A series of additional agreements were also signed, though Egyptian officials did not provide details.
'Independent foreign policy'
Beijing is eyeing a greater foothold in the Middle East, at a time when "the United States looks like it can't really make up its mind whether it wants to withdraw from the region or be more engaged", Mirette Mabrouk, a senior fellow at the Washington-based Middle East Institute, told AFP.
China sees Egypt as a key partner and an entry point to more regional influence.
For Egypt, closer ties with China are part of a broader effort to diversify partnerships rather than align with a single power, Mabrouk said.
Sisi, in an op-ed published in Egyptian media on Tuesday, highlighted Cairo's "independent foreign policy", days after the Emirati branch of Egypt's second-largest bank, Banque Misr, was targeted by US sanctions.
Washington vowed last month to isolate Iran economically, threatening expanded sanctions that could also hit Chinese banks, among others.
China, a major buyer of Iranian oil, has vowed to safeguard its interests.
In the lead-up to an expected meeting between Xi and US President Donald Trump this month, it has also sought to shore up ties with US-friendly regional nations.
Cairo is one of the largest recipients of US military aid, and historically a key Middle East mediator.
Egypt – which under Sisi's administration became one of the world's top weapons buyers – hosted major joint air combat exercises with the Chinese military in August, featuring Beijing's powerful J-16 fighter jet.
China is a major exporter to Egypt, with its trade surplus reaching $12 billion in the first seven months of 2026, according to Chinese customs data.
Across Cairo, a megalopolis home to over 26 million people, major streets have been lined with Chinese and Egyptian flags, as well as billboards showing Sisi and Xi.
Xi is expected to head to the Grand Egyptian Museum overlooking the Giza Pyramids later on Wednesday.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Iran threatens tougher strategy after US strikes kill 4 at wedding
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran threatens tougher strategy after US strikes kill 4 at wedding
Iran threatened to take a tougher line in its war with the United States on Wednesday after the heaviest exchanges in weeks left at least 19 Iranians dead, including four at a wedding -- an incident slammed as a "war crime" by Tehran.
A wave of Iranian attacks earlier targeted US bases in Jordan, the UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain and Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan region, after extensive US bombardment hit sites across Iran.
The flare-up deepens the ongoing impasse in the war, as Iran maintains a stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz oil export route and the US presses its counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Iran reacted with fury after the Iranian Red Crescent said four people including a child were killed and more than 50 people wounded by a US attack that hit a wedding in Iran's south.
"The truth of this unlawful war of choice -- and the true face of the war crime -- is in Sirik, where a wedding ceremony was brutally bombed as part of America's desperate struggle to conceal its failure," foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei posted on X.
The US military did not address the incident directly.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesman Tim Hawkins said "the US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC", referring to Iran's Revolutionary Guards.
Iran's security chief warned the United States would face a "new strategy" from Tehran in the six-month war.
"You will soon see that Iran's new strategy on the battlefield, in diplomacy and in confronting the economic blockade will shatter your foundations," Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei wrote on X.
'Acts like Satan'
Iran's top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf lashed out at Washington over the wedding attack, calling the United States "Satan".
"If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan, and kills like Satan, it's Satan," he posted on X.
The latest round of fighting began when Washington hit Iranian targets on Sunday, the first known strikes in several weeks.
Tehran's forces then targeted US troops in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, and projectiles struck two oil tankers in unclaimed attacks, one of which killed two Filipino sailors, according to a Saudi shipping company.
Trump said the US strikes were "in retaliation for the Iranians' failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait" and for firing missiles at the base in Jordan.
More US strikes came on Tuesday, with Iranian state TV reporting explosions along the Hormuz and on an island in the Gulf, as well as an attack on an airport in the southern province of Kerman.
Seven people were killed and eight others wounded in a missile attack in the southern Khuzestan province, IRNA reported.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said four personnel were killed in a US strike in Kermanshah province, and three paramilitaries died on Lavan island in the Gulf. Another paramilitary was killed in the southern province of Fars, Iranian media said.
US President Donald Trump had warned of "much harder" attacks if Iran retaliated.
But Tehran's response was widespread, and included attacks targeting US interests in Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan, and a US Marine training camp in Jordan near the Saudi and Israeli borders, according to Iranian media.
In the Gulf, air raid sirens sounded in Bahrain and Kuwait, where authorities said an Iranian drone set off a blaze at a residential complex.
'Very saddening'
Iranians expressed regret at the return to hostilities, including the deaths at the wedding. Hossein Moazami, 50, who is self-employed, called the attacks "truly distressing".
"I hope they all return to the negotiating table, because the only people suffering from this are the Iranian people," he said.
"The Americans are on the other side of the world, and nothing happens to them."
A video shared by an Iranian government account showed debris and damage at what it said was the wedding site in Sirik following the US strike, with people heard screaming in the background.
"It is a very saddening incident... Thank God the casualties were not higher," Ali Mallahi, father of the bride and owner of the building that was hit, said in a video carried by state TV.
The war began in late February with US-Israeli attacks on Iran that killed its supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
A fragile ceasefire collapsed after attacks on commercial ships in the Hormuz strait, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed.
Incidents in the strait have continued. Iran's Guards said Wednesday that two oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines due to "the urging of the US military to transit via an illegal route".

articles.title: China’s Xi urges new Middle East security framework during rare Egypt visit
articles.body:
China’s Xi urges new Middle East security framework during rare Egypt visit
Chinese, Egyptian leaders discuss the US-Israel war on Iran, wich has prompted regional powers to rethink defence.
Chinese President Xi Jinping has called on Middle East countries to oppose external influence and consider reshaping the region’s security order.

Xi said China “stands ready to work with countries in the region to safeguard the security of international shipping lanes, advance development cooperation … and eliminate the breeding grounds for conflict”.

The diplomatic campaign comes before an expected meeting between Xi and US President Donald Trump this month.
Cairo is one of the largest recipients of US military aid, receiving $1.3bn annually, and has historically served as a key Middle East mediator.
Xi’s visit also comes after Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan last month signed the Mecca Defence Alliance. Experts have said the move demonstrates a desire by regional countries to diversify their security arrangements beyond Washington.

The pact contains a NATO-style Article 5 clause, meaning an armed attack on any of the three member states is considered an attack on all.
Officials in Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have stressed the pact is not meant to replace any pre-existing security deals.

articles.title: Russian attack cuts power in Odesa region as strikes on Kyiv enter seventh day
articles.body:
Russian drones crash into central Kyiv in seventh day of strikes
KYIV, Sept 2 - Russian drones tore into central Kyiv on Wednesday morning, wounding nine people and damaging residential and university buildings on the seventh day of nearly round-the-clock attacks that have upended daily life in the city.
Moscow's new air campaign against the Ukrainian capital and surrounding region has killed dozens of civilians and disrupted logistics as Kyiv struggles to shoot down the jet-powered drones that have swarmed the area in waves.
Wednesday's attack on a downtown university took place while students were in class, forcing some 160 to seek shelter, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said.
The mounting attacks come as Ukraine braces for a new season of Russian strikes on energy infrastructure, amid a critical shortage of U.S.-designed missile interceptors needed to down Moscow's ballistic missiles.
Earlier on Wednesday, Russia struck power facilities in the southern Odesa region with missiles and drones, authorities said, knocking out power to more than 350,000 homes.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said late on Tuesday he had ordered his forces to prepare the new campaign of "massive" strikes.
"Unfortunately, there has been far too little response from the world and its most influential leaders to this latest Russian escalation of strikes," Zelenskiy wrote on X.
Two people were also killed and eight wounded in Russian strikes on the southeastern city of Dnipro, the regional governor said, where food warehouses and educational buildings were damaged.
TRANSPORTATION SNARLED, PARLIAMENT PUSHED UNDERGROUND
Loud explosions thundered through central Kyiv on Wednesday morning as air defences targeted incoming drones.
While launched in small numbers, the drones have sparked frequent air-raid alerts that have snarled public transportation and forced lawmakers underground.
Parts of the city's Soviet-era metro system are suspended during alerts, making residents such as 27-year-old Maksym walk, scramble for taxis or rely on electric scooters to get to work.
"We need to find a solution," he told Reuters amid the cacophony of morning traffic. "The sooner, the better."
The alerts interrupted parliament twice on Wednesday, prompting lawmakers to test a new digital voting system from underneath the legislature, according to opposition deputy Yaroslav Zhelezniak, who posted footage of the platform.
Earlier this week, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said his city's defence council had appealed to the government to ease the wartime curfew and other traffic restrictions during alerts. REUTERS

articles.title: US strikes wedding party in southern Iran: What we know so far
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US strikes wedding party in southern Iran: What we know so far
Iran accused the United States of striking a wedding gathering in the country’s south, killing five people, including a child, and injuring dozens more in an attack on a residential area near the Strait of Hormuz in Kuhestak, in Sirik county of Hormozgan province, on Tuesday night.
The Red Crescent said shrapnel from a US missile struck the residential property, killing five people and injuring more than 50. Six-year-old Amir Mohammad Karimi was among those killed, it said, adding that those wounded had been transferred to hospital in the nearby city of Minab.
Earlier, Reza Shahidiyan, the governor of Sirik county, told the IRIB state broadcaster that 63 people had been injured, including 50 women and children. Other Iranian reporting has cited as many as 68 wounded.
Videos circulated by Iranian rescue workers showed debris scattered across the site and extensive damage to several buildings, including blown-out walls and windows. Another video posted by the Red Crescent showed a large whole on the roof of a residential building, supposedly from the site of the impact.
Kuhestak lies in Sirik county, on Iran’s southern coast along the strategic Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of global seaborne oil trade passes. The attack came during a large new wave of US strikes across Iran, following more than a month without a direct exchange of fire between Washington and Tehran.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said its forces had launched strikes against targets linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, citing what it called recent attempted attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and on US personnel in the region.
But Washington has not publicly identified the precise target near the wedding site, disclosed the weapon used, or explained how a missile strike came to send lethal shrapnel into a home packed with civilians celebrating a wedding. Earlier reports suggested a telecommunications tower in the Kuhestak area may have been among the targets.
US response
The US did not deny carrying out strikes in the area. Asked about reports of civilian casualties, CENTCOM spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins said: "We’re aware of the reports, which originated from Iranian state media," claiming that "The US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC."
The statement does not address whether the strike hit a civilian residence, whether US planners knew a wedding was under way, whether the house was within the expected blast radius of an intended target, or whether CENTCOM is investigating the deaths and injuries reported by emergency workers and local officials.
The US assertion that it does not target civilians sits uneasily alongside mounting reports of civilian harm from its campaign in Iran. On 28 February, a strike on a girls’ school in Minab, also in Hormozgan province, killed more than 150 people, most of them children, according to Iranian authorities and rights groups.
Washington has yet to publicly accept responsibility or release a final account of that attack. However, a preliminary US military assessment concluded that US forces were likely responsible and that the school was not the intended target. The reported explanation was that outdated intelligence had wrongly classified the site, or the surrounding area, as associated with an Iranian military installation.
Iranian condemnation
Iranian officials condemned the Sirik attack as an assault on civilians and said the country would respond.
Foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran would respond "with firmness", while Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s top negotiator and parliamentary speaker, described the United States as the "Great Satan" and linked the wedding deaths to what he called a broader pattern of US attacks on civilians.
The head of the Iranian Red Crescent Society sent a letter to the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court on Wednesday regarding the wedding attack, assuring prosecutors that the organisation was documenting the effects of the attack in order to "collect and record (them) for follow-up through legal and international channels," calling for an independent investigation into Tuesday's deadly incident.
Iranian officials also said electricity and telephone services had been disrupted in the area, amid reports that US strikes had targeted telecommunications infrastructure in Hormozgan province. Restoration work was under way, according to Iran’s health ministry.
The strike was followed by Iranian missile and drone attacks directed towards US-linked targets and allies across the region, including Bahrain, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and Jordan. The exchange marked one of the sharpest escalations in weeks in the six-month conflict.

articles.title: Xi meets with Sisi in first Egypt visit in a decade
articles.body:
President Xi Jinping on Wednesday met with his Egyptian counterpart, Abdel Fattah El-Sisi as he began his first visit to Egypt in a decade.
The 21-gun salute at Cairo's Ittihadiya Palace marked the start of a day of talks expected to cover the Middle East war and its fallout, including on maritime trade security, as well as boosting investment in the Arab world's most populous country.
The two Brics members are expected to sign a slate of economic agreements, including on artificial intelligence, transport and manufacturing.
Egypt currently estimates Chinese investments at around US$10 billion. 
Beijing has key stakes in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, which are only expected to grow as the US-Iran war threatens global maritime trade.
China has also played a key role in Egypt's megaprojects, the crowning jewel of which is the New Administrative Capital 50 kilometres east of Cairo, large swathes of which have been bankrolled by Chinese investment.
China is a major exporter to Egypt, with its trade surplus reaching US$12 billion in the first seven months of 2026, according to Chinese customs data.
Across Cairo, a megalopolis home to over 26 million people, major streets have been lined with Chinese and Egyptian flags, as well as billboards showing Sisi and Xi.
Street signs boast of "generations of Egyptian-Chinese friendship flowing like the Nile River", while residents have been warned to plan for substantial traffic delays on their commutes.
Xi is expected to traverse the entire capital during his visit on Wednesday, including a stop at the Grand Egyptian Museum overlooking the Giza Pyramids.
According to analysts, Cairo will use the summit to underscore its strategic autonomy, showing it can leverage its close ties with both Washington and Beijing.
Sisi, in an op-ed published in Egyptian media on Tuesday, highlighted Cairo's "independent foreign policy", days after a branch of Egypt's second-largest bank was targeted by US sanctions.
He wrote that Egypt and China were partners in "strengthening the role of the Global South" in an increasingly polarised world. 
Xi's visit is the second leg of his second overseas trip this year, following his participation in a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan where he spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin and others.
In commentary published by Xinhua, Xi said the two countries were "close brothers standing by each other" in the face of imperialism and colonialism and that he looked forward to exploring a deeper partnership. (Xinhua/Agencies)
Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: American forces strike IRGC targets in Iran
articles.body:
US forces have carried out a wave of strikes against Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targets inside Iran, hitting air defence sites, radar systems, maritime assets and other military facilities, according to US Central Command.
CENTCOM announced on 1 September that the strikes had been completed against a range of Iranian military targets. Targets identified by CENTCOM included Iranian air defence positions and radar systems, along with maritime assets and facilities, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites.
CENTCOM stated: “U.S. forces struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites.”
The command added: “The strikes follow recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members.”
The Strait of Hormuz is the narrow maritime passage connecting the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea. It is used by commercial shipping operating between Gulf ports and international markets and is also regularly patrolled by US and allied naval forces.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps maintains its own naval, aerospace and ground forces alongside Iran’s regular armed forces. Its naval element operates extensively in and around the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz. The target set identified by CENTCOM covered several elements of Iranian military infrastructure. Air defence and radar installations form part of Iran’s ability to detect and respond to aircraft and other aerial activity, while communications sites support military command and coordination.
CENTCOM also specifically identified mine-laying capabilities among the targets attacked. Iranian forces have long maintained naval mine capabilities for operations in the waters around Iran, including approaches to the Strait of Hormuz.
The United States currently has more than 50,000 military personnel deployed across the Middle East, according to CENTCOM. US Central Command is responsible for American military operations across a region covering the Middle East and parts of Central and South Asia, including the Persian Gulf and surrounding waters.

articles.title: Trump Suggests Renaming Strait of Hormuz the 'Trump Strait' Amid Renewed Iran Hostilities
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has suggested renaming the Strait of Hormuz the “Trump Strait” amid renewed hostilities with Iran following a brief period of respite.
“Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to Trump Strait? Like America itself, it would be ‘hotter’ than ever before!” the President said Wednesday.
Trump floated the idea a day after the U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) launched a new wave of strikes against Iranian military targets.
The U.S. military said it struck air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
Iran’s Foreign Ministry on Wednesday released a statement insisting the U.S. had attacked civilian areas and service infrastructure in the provinces of Khuzestan, Sistan and Baluchestan, Hormozgan, and Kerman. It said a wedding ceremony in Kuhestak, Sirik County, had been struck, resulting in fatalities and injuries.
In a statement to TIME, CENTCOM spokesperson Navy Captain Tim Hawkins said: “We are aware of reports, which originated from Iranian state media. The U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC.”
The IRGC said it had launched retaliatory strikes on U.S. bases in Jordan, Kuwait, and Bahrain, alongside an additional U.S. facility in Iraq, overnight Tuesday.
The renewed hostilities and threats come after a roughly month-long pause in active hostilities between the two countries. On Sunday, the U.S. military struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island it said were preparing to fire rockets carrying naval mines into the Strait.
Trump’s attempt to rename the Strait underscores how both Iran and the U.S. have continued to vie for control of the vital waterway, through which roughly a fifth of global oil transited before the war.
The President has previously turned to name changes as a show of power and a way to undermine his perceived adversaries, most recently renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America” during the U.S. trade war with Canada.
Meanwhile, although Trump has claimed the U.S. has near total control of the Strait, the tussle over the body of water—which reignited after both countries adopted different interpretations of the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)—rages on.
With no clear path to a negotiated truce, Washington has doubled down on its “economic D-Day” threats against Tehran, increasing the pressure by tightening sanctions in addition to military action.
Traffic falls once more amid renewed instability for the Strait of Hormuz
The latest round of strikes between the U.S. and Iran has further disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
Kpler, a commodities data and analytics firm, shared data with TIME that shows only six ships crossed the Strait on Tuesday—a drop from 19 vessels on Friday last week.
Before the Iran war began on Feb. 28, 138 vessels typically passed through the vital trade waterway during a 24-hour period.
On Wednesday, U.K. Maritime Operations (UKMTO) reported an attack on a tanker transiting the Strait that resulted in two casualties.
Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry reported that Iran had targeted a Saudi tanker in the waterway, with UKMTO later stating that two crew members had been killed.
Iran's Gulf neighbors condemn Tehran's “heinous” retaliatory attacks
The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) described Iran’s overnight retaliatory strikes against U.S. bases in the region as a “heinous” act. Secretary General Jasem Mohamed AlBudaiwi said "these Iranian attacks represent a blatant violation of state sovereignty and a direct threat to their security and stability."
He stated that the GCC stands “firmly alongside” these countries “in all measures and actions taken to preserve their sovereignty, protect their security and stability, and ensure the safety of their peoples and residents.”
The council is made up of six countries on the Arabian Peninsula: Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
The UAE, which suspended trade with Iran in August amid missile strikes, released its own statement condemning Iran’s strikes across the wider Gulf region.
“These hostile attacks constitute a flagrant violation of the sovereignty of the brotherly nations and a threat to their security and stability,” said the UAE’S Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Wednesday.

articles.title: Doubling of F-15EX Fleet Comes with Risks for USAF to Manage: New Pentagon Report
articles.body:
The Air Force’s decision to more than double its purchase of F-15EX Eagle II jets may bolster the service’s fighter fleet, but it also comes with risks and questions officials will have to manage in the years ahead, a new Pentagon report warns.
Earlier this year, Air Force officials announced plans to expand its planned F-15EX fleet from 129 to 267 jets, as they move recapitalize the older F-15E Strike Eagle. When the change was announced as part of the fiscal 2027 budget rollout, the Air Force said it needed to buy more F-15EXs alongside F-35As because both jets bring different capabilities that will be needed in in a future war.
Yet in the F-15EX’s selected acquisition report released in August, program officials noted “new cost and schedule uncertainties” that come with the increase they’re trying to mitigate.
Boeing declined to comment on the concerns raised in the acquisition report. The Air Force did not immediately respond to a query.
One concern is how the expanded procurement plan will play out over time. The previous F-15EX acquisition strategy called for eight lots of the jet; the new one calls for 12. This will likely require Boeing to conduct “a major technical refresh” to overcome diminishing manufacturing sources and material shortages, the report states.
Eventually, key systems such as the F-15EX’s radar, mission computer, electronic warfare suite, and engines could become obsolete and need to be replaced. This “constitutes a significant redesign effort,” the report states.
The program’s method for managing this risk involves testing and integrating those upgraded subsystems as part of future operational flight program releases now scheduled for between 2031 and 2035.
“This provides a structured, risk-reduced pathway for flight testing and fielding these new capabilities without causing a gap in the production line,” the report said.
Another concern is uncertainty around the costs of extending production. Program officials say they have not yet fully estimated those costs, though they has begun a rapid cost estimation process to inform the fiscal 2028 budget request. Until then, the EX program is using government estimates for its initial budget sizing, while “commissioning formal studies to obtain preliminary cost and schedule estimates from the contractors,” the report said.
The report also highlighted schedule issues that will need to be worked through in the short and long term. Parts and material shortages risk slowing the production of F-15EX jets in Lot 2 and beyond, officials wrote, noting that some of the most acute shortages including the jet’s Elbit-made large area displays and low-profile heads-up displays, General Electric F110 engines, and Collins-made cartridges for ejection systems.
Those shortages were mitigated for Lot 1B largely by stocking up on supplies during the production halt caused by a factory strike from August to November 2025—but the risks remain for future lots, the report said. The Pentagon is taking actions to keep the F-15EX’s production schedule on track, such as by putting borrowing and payback agreements in place with foreign military sales customers to maintain the supply of crucial parts.
But the strike at Boeing’s St. Louis, Mo., plant that makes the F-15EX has permanently set the jet behind schedule, the report said. Boeing’s F-15EX contract requires it to deliver all 12 Lot 3 jets in early calendar 2026, but due to the strike, the report said the company will only be able to deliver six of those jets by the end of 2026.
These “unrecoverable delays” are having cascading effects on the Air Force’s plans to field the Eagle II. The acquisition report notes the 142nd Wing of the Oregon Air National Guard will not receive all of its F-15EXs from Lot 2 until at least mid-2026, and the first Lot 3 F-15EXs, meant to be stationed overseas, will not be fielded until at least the first quarter of fiscal 2027, the report said.
These oversea jets will be stationed at Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, Japan. Kadena previously had F-15C and D Eagle fighters, but the Air Force started retiring those aging fighters in November 2022. Since then, a steady stream of other fighters have rotated through Kadena. The planned permanent force of F-15EXs, which were originally supposed to start arriving in spring 2026, have been delayed into 2027.
The F-15EX program management office is working with the Defense Department’s Business Operators for National Defense, or BOND, team to figure out how to optimize the F-15EX production schedule and prioritize the Lot 3 jets planned for overseas assignments as they go through the final assembly process, the report said.
The program office is also working with Air Combat Command and the National Guard Bureau to create a coordinated bridging strategy, that makes sure older jets or alternate force structures are available to cover the Air Force’s operational requirements, until the F-15EXs arrive.
The fourth lot of F-15EXs is also already behind schedule, according to the report. Boeing should have started delivering those jets in 2026, the report said, but they are now not expected to start arriving until calendar 2028. Boeing has to increase its F-15EX production rate to two per month to meet its delivery requirements, the report said.

articles.title: Ukrainian attacks fueling global ‘energy shock’ – US Treasury secretary (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Ukrainian attacks fueling global ‘energy shock’ – US Treasury secretary (VIDEO)
Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure have fueled a global “energy shock” and pushed prices higher, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent claimed. The disruption has compounded strains caused by the Iran war, he added.
Ukraine has ramped up long-range drone strikes against Russia’s energy sector this year, targeting oil refineries, storage facilities, and export infrastructure deep inside the country. Kiev says the campaign is aimed at weakening Russia’s ability to finance and maintain its military operations.
Speaking to Fox on Wednesday, Bessent said the world is experiencing an energy shock partly because of the Ukrainian strikes.
”Ukraine has decided that they want to blow up Russian energy assets and refined products,” which is “creating upward price pressure on a global basis,” he said.
Bessent:
We are going through an energy shock right now.
Ukraine has decided that they want to blow up Russian energy assets. 
That is creating price pressure on a global basis. pic.twitter.com/oXGhLQY2FN
The strikes have significantly disrupted Russian refining, according to energy analytics firm Kpler. It said last week that refinery runs fell to around 3.8 million barrels per day in July, their lowest level in more than two decades. Refined-product exports dropped to around 1.2 million barrels per day, down from 2.3 million a year earlier.
Moscow has accused Kiev of increasingly targeting civilian infrastructure amid Ukrainian setbacks on the battlefield. Russia has retaliated with massive drone and missile strikes on Ukraine’s military-linked infrastructure and shipping facilities, effectively crippling the country’s main export route through its Black Sea ports.
The Iran war has also strained global energy markets, according to Bessent. Before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February, around a fifth of global energy supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran’s subsequent restrictions on commercial shipping, coupled with the US naval blockade, have disrupted flows and pushed prices higher.
Washington has stepped up economic pressure on Tehran. Bessent warned on Sunday that the US could unleash “financial violence” against Iran, threatening new secondary sanctions every week against Tehran and those doing business with it.

articles.title: Zelensky warns airlines Russian skies not safe due to Ukraine drones
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned Tuesday that his country's drones would make Russia's airspace "completely unsafe" for the duration of the war, drawing accusations of "state terrorism" from Russian leader Vladimir Putin. Speaking with FRANCE 24's Mark Owen, Former British Military Intelligence Officer Philip Ingram explains that Zelensky's warning is addressed to "those international airlines from the Middle East, from South East Asia, China included that are still operating into Moscow" adding that "it's all part of the information war and bringing the overall conflict to the Russian people".

articles.title: Trump nominates loyalist Hung Cao to be permanent navy secretary – US politics live
articles.body:
Trump: 'Canada has been ripping off the United States for many, many years'
The resumption of US-Canada trade talks does not seem to be on the horizon. During a press conference with US travel executives, Trump was asked if negotiations would resume.
“Canada has been ripping off the United States for many, many years, for decades, many decades,” Trump said, adding shortly thereafter, “It’s a very unfair deal. They charge tremendous tariffs to our farmers. They take advantage of our farmers. They take advantage of our tourists. They take advantage of airlines.”
The collapse of discussions resulted in Trump imposing 50% tariffs on $20bn in Canadian goods and Canada threatening retaliatory tariffs starting 8 September.
Democratic lawmakers in the House introduced a war powers resolution on Wednesday seeking to stop the Trump administration’s boat strikes.
The US military has killed at least 227 people in 68 strikes in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific since last year as part of a campaign against what it describes as “narcoterrorists” to stop the flow of drugs into the US.
The UN and other humanitarian groups have said the attacks are extrajudicial killings.
Lawmakers Gregory W Meeks, Adam Smith, Jim Himes and and Bennie G Thompson, the group that introduced the resolution, said in a statement that people have been killed “without due process or a credible national-security justification”. Congress has never authorized the attacks, the group wrote.
“A year later, the administration has little to show for this lawless campaign except a mounting body count, a massive price tag, and a stain on the American conscience,” the lawmakers said.
“Time and again, this administration has refused to use the military responsibly or consult with Congress, even though the American people have made clear they do not want their tax dollars being spent on more endless military campaigns. It’s time for this failed campaign to end.”
The Pentagon has introduced guidelines for the mandatory new testosterone deficiency screening required for service members age 30 and older, a policy introduced by Pete Hegseth last month.
The defense secretary announced the mandate in July, stating that the program would “[ensure] you have the right testosterone levels to operate at your absolute best”.
The guidance will go into effect immediately and require testosterone blood tests for men 30 and older. The guidance does not require the tests for younger men or women of any age, though Reuters reports it calls for screening of symptoms, including disrupted menstrual cycles, that are linked to hormonal dysregulation.
Doctors have questioned the scientific basis for the policy.
Senator Richard Blumenthal has pushed back against a statement from the US Postal Service about its new system to screen millions of mail-in ballots for the upcoming midterm elections.
This week it emerged a whistleblower told Congress that the system was hastily thrown together and that a single glitch in scanning could result in whole ballot batches being turned away. Blumenthal said the system, which came after Donald Trump’s executive order tightening federal control over mail-in voting, was “perilously rushed and potentially unlawful”.
In response, the postal service said it was “carefully reviewing the concerns”, but that it had spent months developing the federal ballot mail portal and it was done “in a manner consistent with court orders”.
Blumenthal said on Wednesday that “absolutely nothing” in the statement “denies or contradicts the deeply disturbing details of the whistleblower’s disclosure”.
“Most importantly, it does nothing to directly address the fears of voters that USPS will refuse to deliver their ballots based on the output of a shoddy computer system they started building four months ago,” he said. “‘Just trust us’ is not acceptable.”
Congressman James Comer said the US Department of Justice is investigating Ilhan Omar and her “entire family”.
In an interview with the rightwing podcaster Benny Johnson, the chair of the House oversight committee referenced a “discrepancy” on a financial disclosure form and said the Minnesota congresswoman was seeking “earmarks for things that would have benefited the Somali community that have already been identified in committing fraud in Minnesota”.
Omar has long been the subject of attacks and criticism from the politicians on the right, including JD Vance, who have accused the representative of immigration fraud, among other accusations. The Democrat has also frequently faced xenophobic attacks from Donald Trump.
Earlier this year a man sprayed her with vinegar as while was speaking at an event. She told the Guardian in December 2025 that she faced no death threats during Joe Biden’s presidency, but that changed when Trump returned to office.
“Now they are back up, and so there is a clear correlation between [Trump’s] presidency and the political violence that we see and the political danger that a lot of members of Congress and electeds feel across the country,” she said at the time.
US judge blocks Trump's newest order limiting birthright citizenship
A US judge has blocked Donald Trump’s latest effort to restrict birthright citizenship.
Deborah Boardman issued a preliminary injunction, preventing the Trump administration from enforcing the president’s new executive order, which he signed after the US Supreme Court rejected a previous effort.
The new order targets so-called “birth tourism”, and seeks to make children of people who work for foreign governments and those classified as an “alien enemy”, among other groups, ineligible for automatic citizenship.
Boardman said the order was “almost certainly unconstitutional”.
“This Court must, once again, preliminarily enjoin enforcement of the President’s most recent attempt to strip the right to citizenship from them,” she wrote.
Patagonia, the outdoor clothing and gear company, has joined a lawsuit challenging Donald Trump’s decision to significantly reduce the Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments in Utah, removing protections from nearly 3m acres.
In July, the president approved the reduction of the sites by 90%, clearing the way to open the land to oil and gas companies. He argued in his proclamations that doing so would allow lands to be “put to a higher-priority use” and that they contained critical minerals important to “ resource independence …[and] national security”.
Patagonia said it was joining the lawsuit to put a stop to what it described as illegal orders that “betray Tribal sovereignty”.
“We will not stand idly by while anti-public lands crusaders attempt to exploit these lands for their extractive-industry friends or disrespect tribal nations,” Ryan Gellert, the company’s CEO, said in a statement.
House Democrats rejected a constitutional amendment proposed by Republicans to ensure the size of the supreme court is permanently capped at nine justices. It failed 212-206.
As Reuters pointed out, the proposal was part of a Republican effort to make the supreme court a campaign issue ahead of the November midterms. The GOP was quick to seize on the issue with the National Republican Congressional Committee claiming in a statement that House Democrats “want to pack the Supreme Court with liberal justices so they can follow through on their radical socialist agenda”.
“Give House Democrats an ounce of power, and they’ll use every bit of it to fundamentally transform America into an unrecognizable socialist hellscape,” spokesperson Mike Marinella said.
Congressman Jamie Raskin argued Republicans were seeking to “cement their stacked and packed MAGA Supreme Court majority into the Constitution and strip away yet another basic power the Framers gave to Congress”.
“After sycophantically surrendering to Donald Trump our war powers, spending powers, tariff powers, and powers over federal buildings, to name a few, now they want to give up a power we have had since the Republic was founded: the power to decide how many Justices will be on the Supreme Court.”
DSA of LA endorses Nithya Raman in mayoral race against Karen Bass
Nithya Raman, the progressive Los Angeles city councillor challenging Mayor Karen Bass, has received an endorsement from the city’s chapter Democratic Socialists of America.
The Los Angeles Times reported on Wednesday that the organization endorsed Raman after more than 60% of voters in an online election among chapter members backed her for mayor.
The decision came after significant debate given her relationship with the chapter – she has long been a DSA member but the organization censured her in 2024 for pursuing an endorsement from a Democrats for Israel group. The DSA LA endorsement is expected to boost Raman’s campaign, as the organization has a significant volunteer base.
Raman beat out reality TV personality Spencer Pratt to advance to the November election against her former political ally Bass.
Donald Trump celebrated the news that Apple had fulfilled his request to rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America” for Maps app users in the US following an executive order that came amid rising trade tensions between the US and Canada.
“Apple Maps has just announced that it has changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, so now that very important change of names, between Google Maps and Apple Maps, is complete, ratified, and binding,” Trump said in a post online on Wednesday afternoon.
It’s unclear what the president meant by “ratified” and “binding”.
Arizona DemocratAdelita Grijalva has slammed new border wall construction near Quitobaquito Springs on the Tohono O’odham Nation’s ancestral lands.
“This morning, bulldozers are tearing through protected lands to make way for Trump’s second border wall — just 0.7 miles east of Quitobaquito Springs and getting closer,” Grijalva said in a statement, which included a link to video apparently showing this construction. “This is tribal land. It does not belong to Trump.”
Grijalva said that authorities and private contractors had gone onto sovereign tribal lands despite objections from the Tohono O’odham Nation.
“This level of disrespect is shameful and will go down as a stain on our nation’s history and its treatment of Indigenous Peoples,” Grijalva’s statement also said. “This isn’t just about a wall.
“It’s about erasing people, cultures, and bulldozing over tribal sovereignty.”
Department of Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin said he was on a plane that made an emergency landing.
Mullin’s disclosure was in an X post on Wednesday that shared another account’s description of this incident.
“A Coast Guard aircraft has landed safely at DCA after declaring an emergency in the air C101 had lost its right engine mid-flight and diverted to Reagan Airport for an immediate landing. All 14 members on board have landed safely,” @TheDMVLive posted just before 2 pm local time.
Just over an hour later, Mullin posted: “The United States Coast Guard pilots made the single engine landing feel routine. No panic, just straight professionalism. After we landed, the pilots told me that was a first for them! We could not have been in better hands.”
The Trump administration rejected New York’s request for help related to a major snowstorm that caused $168m in damage, governor Kathy Hochul said.
“Another day, another denial of critical federal assistance for New York by the Trump Administration,” Hochul said in a statement Wednesday. “Just one day after calling out President Trump and Secretary Mullin for continuing to withhold $87 million in counterterrorism funding, my Administration was informed today that FEMA has officially denied our appeal for a Major Disaster Declaration following the February blizzard that caused more than $168 million in damages and placed a serious financial burden on communities across New York City, Long Island and the Mid-Hudson.”
“This storm met every FEMA threshold for federal assistance, yet the Trump Administration continues to play political games and betray every New Yorker who believes that the federal government is there to protect and support them,” Hochul also said. “By refusing to intervene and grant our request, President Trump has told every New Yorker who weathered this major storm and the first responders, utility crews and emergency management staff who worked tirelessly to keep our communities safe that you do not matter to him.”
“But let’s be clear, Republican members of Congress across New York are also enabling this neglect,” Hochul also said. “Their continued silence and refusal to break with the President is a direct betrayal of the communities they were elected to serve.”
“It is past time these members of congress demand that the President grant this disaster declaration and deliver every dollar of relief their constituents are owed.”
The Guardian has reached out to The White House and FEMA for comment.
Trump: 'happy about' Harry and Meghan returning to UK, says he 'was not a fan'
President Trump has weighed in on the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s move to Britain, saying at a press conference that: “I’m happy about it”.
“I was not a fan,” Trump said in response to a reporter’s query, during a question-and-answer session following a press conference with travel executives. “I had a very good relationship with the Queen, really good. I got to know her very well. A really good relationship with King Charles – I knew him as Prince Charles and King Charles. I’ve known him for a long time.”
Trump, describing Charles as a “great, great guy,” said he thought Prince Harry and Meghan Markle “treated the royal family with great disrespect.”
“I didn’t like it,” he also said, adding, “ If I were the royal family, I would not have taken them back.”
The couple’s move back to England comes six years after they left for the US. The King is reportedly looking forward to spending more time with them in a personal capacity, but Harry and Meghan will remain private individuals as they previously gave up their official royal duties.

articles.title: Moscow likely behind drone-factory arson, says Poland’s Tusk
articles.body:
A military operator launches a FlyEye WB Electronics SA, a Polish reconnaissance drone, bought in the frame of program 'The Army of Drones' during test flights in the Kyiv region on August 2, 2022. | Sergei Supinsky/AFP via Getty Images
The fire at a Polish drone factory supplying weapons to Ukraine was "deliberate arson," and Russia is likely behind the attack, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said at a cabinet meeting Wednesday.
WB Electronics, where the fire broke out on Monday morning, is one of Poland’s largest private defense companies. It produces reconnaissance drones and loitering munitions, including FlyEye and Warmate, used by Ukraine against Russian forces. The fire was soon extinguished, leaving no casualties, Polish radio reported.
“This is a continuation of Russia’s escalatory actions throughout the region,” the Polish leader said, adding that "unfortunately, these are not the first cases and, even worse, they certainly won’t be the last."
Advertisement
On the same day of the attack, Polish prosecutors classified the incident as a “terrorist crime” committed by "foreign intelligence" and involving the “deliberate setting of a fire.”
The incident comes amid an intensification of suspected Russian attacks targeting facilities linked to military production and support for Ukraine.
In Poland, in addition to the event at WB Electronics, a second fire broke out at a JFG Composites facility in Lublin on Sunday — the company produces composite components for the aerospace industry, including parts for aircraft and helicopters.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government on Tuesday accused Russia of being responsible for the incursion and announced retaliatory measures. EU officials backed Germany and called for further visa restrictions.

articles.title: ‘A fever dream’: USS Abraham Lincoln’s crew arrive in Thailand after record stint at sea
articles.body:
At Pattaya’s Hard Rock Cafe and hotel, the city’s mayor and police officials, along with women in traditional Thai dress, waited to greet the sailors who were arriving in civilian clothes, bags slung over their shoulders, off the buses.
The USS Abraham Lincoln’s crew of 5,000 had not been on shore for nearly nine months, a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea.
Crew appeared to have been told not to speak to the gathered journalists about the reportedly deteriorating living conditions onboard but said they were looking forward to being on dry land, sleeping and going home.
One sailor, Breese, who did not want to give his surname, said “it’s a fever dream right now” and he was looking forward to trying Thai food for the first time and meeting new people.
Once a quiet fishing village, Pattaya was transformed during the Vietnam war into one of the most infamous red light districts in the world with the arrival of American troops using military bases in Thailand.
At its peak, tens of thousands of US military personnel came through each year, said Pipatpong Fakfare, an associate professor specialising in tourism at Bangkok University. “In my opinion, it’s really the founding influence for the town. The US military turned a quiet fishing village into a global destination for an international nightlife and entertainment hub in about 15 years,” he said.
Although the American troops left by the mid-70s, the sex industry infrastructure continued to grow, with European tourists taking their place, and more recently waves of Chinese and Russian visitors, Pipatpong said.
The Hard Rock hotel is around the corner from the Soi 6 alley, known for its go-go bars, one of the many areas that contribute to Pattaya’s sex tourism industry. Soi 6 and the neighbouring area would be off-limits for crew after sunset, said Pattaya’s mayor, Poramet Ngampichet.
However, Walking Street, the town’s other entertainment and red light district, was displaying a massive neon sign at its entrance saying: “Pattaya City is pleased to welcome USS Abraham Lincoln carrier and its personnel.”
The sailors were being released in staggered groups, so not everyone was out. Shakeira Fairfax, who had travelled all the way from New Jersey, had to wait one more day to be reunited with her sailor daughter, Jada Fairfax.
Fairfax said she was mostly excited. “I just want to pick her up and spin her around. She’s my baby always,” but, she said, “I don’t know who I’m welcoming home.”
Jada finished her basic training last October and was shipped out a month later, two months before the US and Israel launched their war on Iran. Jada celebrated her 25th birthday onboard in June.
Fairfax said there was an “abrupt” stop to communication when the war broke out, but she had since been able to check in with her intermittently and send care packages.
The ship’s captain, Dan Keeler, acknowledged to the media that the carrier “looks like a dirty car in a parking lot”. As for the reports of the conditions onboard, he said: “I don’t know how to say it other than there’s a disconnect between reporting back home and what’s happening on the ship.”
Keeler added: “First-time sailors are going to complain about the food, the living conditions, similar to sending kids off to college for the first time. We did get caught up in an election cycle and got thrown around like a football.”
Keeler said there was plenty of food on the ship but admitted it became hard to get fresh fruit and vegetables, which stopped being served. “I am looking forward to a fresh salad.” They also had to be careful with supplies of soap and toothpaste to ensure every sailor could receive some, he added.
Asked about the reports of attempted suicides onboard the ship, Keeler did not answer, saying there was an open investigation. As for comments from Donald Trump, which included claims that the 270-day deployment was “not nearly long enough”, Keeler told the Guardian: “The president speaks for himself.”
Crew from the USS Higgins also arrived at the Hard Rock hotel. When asked about the conditions onboard the two vessels, Ethan Johnson, a cook on the Higgins, said: “We joined the military, it’s not a cruise ship.”
Johnson said there was plenty of meat and vegetables onboard the Higgins.
As well as being prohibited from entering certain areas, sailors are also being prevented from doing any water sports in the area, owing to the potential danger.
They will also not be allowed to visit pharmacies as Thai authorities do not want sailors accessing medicines that do not require a prescription in Thailand but may need a prescription in the US, Poramet said.
Kristopher Robinson, a naval attache with the US embassy, said Pattaya was chosen as the destination for rest and relaxation because the “people of Thailand have a history of being wonderful hosts not just to US sailors but people from all around”.
Robinson said the crew would take as much opportunity for rest as possible and conduct themselves in accordance with US and local laws. “Sailors here, like all tourists, they’re going to enjoy Pattaya’s great food and wonderful culture,” he said.

articles.title: US military says it completed latest wave of strikes on Iran
articles.body:
US military says it completed latest wave of strikes on Iran
WASHINGTON, Sept 1 - The U.S. military said late on Tuesday it completed its latest wave of strikes on Iran, saying it struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targets as the Iran war escalated following a weekend exchange of fire.
U.S. forces struck IRGC targets "including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites," the U.S. Central Command said on X.
An Axios report, citing U.S. officials, said the U.S. military attacked two Iranian government tankers in Tuesday's strikes.
Iran retaliated on Tuesday to the barrage of U.S. strikes, as the exchange marked the most serious escalation in weeks in a conflict that has driven up global energy prices.
The strikes followed a weekend exchange of fire, the first since late July, and attacks on Monday on two tankers leaving the Strait of Hormuz, the global oil supply waterway that Iran has effectively closed to shipping. Tehran struck back at U.S. assets in Jordan, Bahrain and Iraq.
Five people were killed and 50 wounded at a wedding near Sirik, a coastal area on the Strait of Hormuz, the Iranian Red Crescent reported. The Mehr news agency said a 4-year-old child was among those killed, while the IRNA news agency, citing a provincial official, put the number of wounded at 68.
The U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on February 28 and Iran responded with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host U.S. bases.
U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed thousands and displaced millions.
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said 17 million barrels of oil transited the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, saying it marked the highest level of crude oil to pass through the waterway since the war had reduced flows.
President Donald Trump said on Tuesday he was "not trying to force Iran to the bargaining table."
"When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?" Trump wrote on social media. REUTERS

Kyiv • UNN
